That is the low-ADH end, after drinking a lot.
Urine at 300 would mean ADH is doing little either way.
No urine concentration can carry 600 mOsm in less than 0.5 L.

questions.q: A patient passes 400 mL a day (oliguria). Where does that volume fall on this graph, and what does it mean?
options: Below the curve’s floor: no urine can carry the day’s solute
On the curve at about 1,500 mOsm/L, which the kidneys can reach with enough ADH
On the plateau, so it is a normal volume
Above the curve, so solute is lost too fast

why.correct: At 400 mL, even maximally concentrated urine carries only 0.4 L × 1,200 mOsm/L = 480 mOsm, less than the 600 made each day, so nitrogen wastes and other solutes accumulate in the blood.
options: Right: 480 mOsm out, 600 made; the rest stays in the blood.
The kidneys cannot concentrate urine past the medulla’s 1,200 mOsm/L.
The curve has no plateau; 0.4 L is below anything it reaches.
Too little volume is the problem here, not too much.

questions.q: A high-protein diet raises the daily solute load to 900 mOsm, mostly urea. How does the curve change?
options: It moves up: the minimum volume rises to 0.75 L
It moves down: the minimum falls to 0.25 L
It does not move, because the kidneys concentrate harder
Only the dilute end moves

why.correct: Volume = solute ÷ concentration. With more solute and the same 1,200 mOsm/L ceiling, the least possible volume is 900 ÷ 1,200 = 0.75 L. More solute means more obligatory urine.
options: Right: more solute, more water needed at every concentration.
More solute cannot need less water.
The ceiling is set by the medulla; it does not rise with the load.
Every point of the curve scales with the solute load.

graphs.title: ATP yield of one glucose, stage by stage
graphs.intro: The ATP made from one glucose broken down fully with oxygen, with each carrier’s ATP credited to the stage that made the carrier (about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2). The wide bars are each stage’s total; the narrow bars inside are the ATP made directly, by substrate-level phosphorylation. Glycolysis gives 5 to 7, depending on which shuttle carries its NADH electrons into the mitochondrion; the bar shows 7.
graphs.alt: Bar graph of ATP per glucose for three stages. Glycolysis: total 5 to 7, drawn at 7, of which 2 are made directly. Pyruvate to acetyl CoA: total 5, none made directly. Citric acid cycle: total 20, of which 2 are made directly. Altogether about 30 to 32 ATP.

questions.q: Read the total ATP credited to the citric acid cycle stage.
questions.why: 20 ATP: 2 made directly, plus 6 NADH × 2.5 = 15 and 2 FADH2 × 1.5 = 3 from the carriers it hands to the electron transport chain.

questions.q: Read the total ATP credited to the step from pyruvate to acetyl CoA.
questions.why: 5 ATP, all of it from the 2 NADH (2 × 2.5) made as the two pyruvate lose a carbon each. The step makes no ATP directly.

questions.q: Add up the narrow bars: how many ATP per glucose are made directly, by substrate-level phosphorylation?
questions.why: 2 in glycolysis plus 2 (by way of GTP) in the citric acid cycle: 4 of the 30 to 32. The other 26 to 28, about 88%, come from oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q: Which stage makes no ATP directly at all?
options: Pyruvate to acetyl CoA
Glycolysis
The citric acid cycle
None: every stage makes some directly

why.correct: The step from pyruvate to acetyl CoA removes a carbon as CO2 and loads NADH, but no phosphate is passed to ADP there. Its 5 ATP all come later, from the electron transport chain.
options: Right: its bar has no narrow bar inside.
Glycolysis passes phosphates to ADP, making 4 and spending 2: a net 2 directly.
The citric acid cycle makes one ATP per turn by way of GTP: 2 per glucose.
One stage makes none directly.

questions.q: Which stage is credited with the most ATP, and mainly how?
options: The citric acid cycle, mostly through its carriers
Glycolysis, through substrate-level phosphorylation
The citric acid cycle, by making ATP directly at each of its eight steps
Pyruvate to acetyl CoA, through the CO2 it releases

why.correct: The cycle stage is credited with 20 of the 30 to 32 ATP, but only 2 are made in the cycle itself; the rest come from its 6 NADH and 2 FADH2 at the electron transport chain.
options: Right: its carriers, not the cycle itself, account for most of its bar.
Glycolysis is credited with only 5 to 7, of which 2 are made directly.
Only one step per turn makes ATP (by way of GTP); the narrow bar is small.
Releasing CO2 makes no ATP; that stage’s ATP comes from its NADH.

questions.q: An older textbook counts 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2 (and 2 or 3 for each NADH from glycolysis, depending on the shuttle). How do the stage totals change?
options: The total becomes about 36 to 38
Only the narrow bars rise
Nothing changes: the carriers are the same
The totals fall, because whole numbers are smaller

why.correct: With 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH2, glycolysis becomes 6 to 8, pyruvate to acetyl CoA 6 and the cycle 24: about 36 to 38 in all. Current measurements of H+ pumped and used give about 2.5 and 1.5, hence 30 to 32. Give 36–38 if your exam expects it.
options: Right: the carriers are worth more in the old count, so every bar that includes them grows.
The ATP made directly does not depend on the carrier values.
The carriers are the same, but each is credited with more ATP.
3 and 2 are larger than 2.5 and 1.5, so the totals rise.

questions.q: Cyanide blocks complex IV of the electron transport chain. Which ATP can a cell still make from glucose?
options: Only the 2 made directly by glycolysis
All but the citric acid cycle’s 20
The 4 made directly in glycolysis and the cycle
None at all

why.correct: With the chain blocked, no carrier yields ATP, and NAD+ and FAD run out in the matrix, so the citric acid cycle stops too, taking its 2 direct ATP with it. Glycolysis continues, regenerating NAD+ by making lactate: 2 ATP per glucose.
options: Right: only glycolysis, with lactate made to keep it running.
The pyruvate and cycle stages depend on the chain to regenerate NAD+, so they stop as well.
The cycle’s direct ATP stops too, because the cycle itself stops without NAD+ and FAD.
Glycolysis still makes 2 ATP, which is why the cell survives for minutes, not seconds.

graphs.title: Fuel use over days of fasting
graphs.intro: A person with normal fat stores who has water but no food. Top: blood ketone bodies. Bottom: the glucose the brain uses and the muscle protein broken down each day. Typical, approximate values.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over 40 days without food. Top: blood ketone bodies rise from about 0.1 mmol/L to about 2 by day 3, 5 by day 10 and level off near 6.5 after three to four weeks. Bottom: brain glucose use stays near 120 grams a day for two days, then falls to about 40 grams a day by four weeks. Muscle protein breakdown is about 75 grams a day on days 2 and 3, then falls to about 20 grams a day by three to four weeks.

hlines.label: low-carbohydrate diets usually stay below this

questions.q: Read the blood ketone body level at day 21.
questions.why: About 6 mmol/L. After a few weeks without food, ketone bodies reach about 5 to 7 mmol/L, yet blood pH stays normal, because a little insulin still limits fat release and buffers take up the H+.

questions.q: Read the glucose the brain uses per day at day 28.
questions.why: About 40 g a day, down from about 120 g. Ketone bodies now supply about two thirds of the brain’s energy.

questions.q: Read the muscle protein broken down per day on day 2.
questions.why: About 75 g a day. With glycogen gone and ketone bodies still low, the liver makes most of the brain’s 120 g of glucose from amino acids released from muscle.

questions.q: During which period is muscle protein broken down fastest, and why?
options: Days 1 to 3, before ketone bodies rise
The first day: liver glycogen is being used
Weeks 3 to 6: fat stores are running out
Throughout: protein breakdown never changes

why.correct: Once liver glycogen runs out, all glucose must be made new, and the brain still needs about 120 g a day. Amino acids are the main source, so muscle protein pays until ketone bodies rise.
options: Right: this is when protein pays for glucose.
On the first day glycogen still supplies much of the glucose.
With normal fat stores, fat is not yet running out at six weeks, and the curve shows protein breakdown low and steady.
The curve falls by about three quarters over the first month.

questions.q: In which period does the brain shift most of its fuel from glucose to ketone bodies?
options: About day 3 to day 21
The first day
After day 30
The brain never uses ketone bodies

why.correct: As ketone bodies climb, the brain takes them up in proportion to their level, and its glucose use falls from about 120 to about 45 g a day over these weeks.
options: Right: brain glucose use falls steeply while ketone bodies rise.
On the first day ketone bodies are still near zero.
By then both curves have leveled off; the switch is already done.
After a few days without food the brain burns ketone bodies, which is what spares protein.

questions.q: Imagine a brain that could not use ketone bodies. How would the muscle protein curve change?
options: It would stay high, near 75 g a day
It would fall faster than normal
It would fall exactly as it does now
It would drop to zero

why.correct: The brain would still need about 120 g of glucose a day, and fatty acids cannot become glucose, so amino acids would keep supplying it. Vital muscle, including heart and breathing muscle, would be used up within a few weeks.
options: Right: without the switch there is no protein sparing.
Nothing would lower the brain’s glucose need, so there is no reason for faster sparing.
The fall in protein breakdown is caused by the brain’s switch to ketone bodies.
Glucose must still come from somewhere; glycerol and lactate cannot supply 120 g a day.

questions.q: The hiker has water with sugar in it, about 100 g of glucose a day, but no other food. How does the ketone curve change?
options: It stays much lower
It rises higher and faster
It is unchanged, because sugar is not fat
It rises above 10 mmol/L, as in ketoacidosis

why.correct: The glucose keeps insulin from falling as far, and insulin brakes lipolysis, so fewer fatty acids reach the liver and fewer ketone bodies are made. The glucose also spares the liver from drawing off as much oxaloacetate to make glucose.
options: Right: some carbohydrate keeps insulin up enough to hold ketogenesis down.
More insulin means less fat breakdown, not more.
Glucose changes the hormones that decide how much fat is broken down.
Ketoacidosis needs insulin to be almost absent; glucose raises insulin.

graphs.title: Heat loss at rest as the air warms
graphs.intro: A lightly dressed adult resting in still air of different temperatures, with core temperature held steady. Heat made at rest stays about 75 kcal an hour; the two lines show how that heat leaves. Schematic, typical values.
graphs.alt: Line graph of heat flow in kcal per hour against air temperature from 15 to 40 °C. Heat made stays flat at about 75. Heat lost by radiation, conduction and convection stays near 60 from 15 to 20 °C (skin vessels narrow in the cooler air), falls to 30 at 30 and zero at 35 °C, and becomes a heat gain of about 22 at 40 °C. Heat lost by evaporation stays near 15 up to 20 °C, then rises to 45 at 30, 75 at 35 and 97 at 40 °C.

questions.q: Read the heat lost by evaporation at 20 °C.
questions.why: About 15 kcal an hour, a fifth of the 75 made. At rest in a cool room, radiation, conduction and convection carry most of the heat away.

questions.q: At what air temperature does dry heat loss (radiation, conduction and convection) fall to zero?
questions.why: About 35 °C, close to skin temperature. Heat flows from warmer to cooler, so once the air is as warm as the skin these routes carry nothing, and above it they add heat.

questions.q: Over which range is evaporation the only way left to lose heat?
options: Above about 35 °C
Below about 25 °C
Only between 25 and 30 °C
At every air temperature

why.correct: Above skin temperature, radiation, conduction and convection run backward and add heat, so evaporation must remove both the heat made and the heat gained.
options: Right: the dry line is below zero here.
In cool air the dry routes carry most of the heat; evaporation is the small share.
Both routes carry heat here.
In cool air evaporation is only about a fifth of the loss.

questions.q: Where does most heat leave by radiation, conduction and convection?
options: In cool air, below about 27 °C
In hot air, above 35 °C
Only at exactly 30 °C
Nowhere: evaporation always carries most

why.correct: In cool air the gradient from skin to surroundings is large, so the dry routes carry most of the heat; radiation alone is about 60% of the loss at rest.
options: Right: the dry line is above the evaporation line here.
Above 35 °C the dry routes add heat instead.
At 30 °C evaporation already carries more than the dry routes.
Evaporation carries only about a fifth of the loss in a cool room.

questions.q: The air is now very humid. How does the evaporation line change in hot air, and what follows?
options: It levels off below the heat made, and core temperature climbs
It rises higher, because humid air carries more heat away from the skin
It is unchanged, because sweat glands still secrete
It moves to cooler temperatures, starting sooner

why.correct: Evaporation needs a water vapor gradient from skin to air. Humid air shrinks it, so sweat drips instead of evaporating. Above skin temperature the loss can no longer match the heat made plus the heat gained, and core temperature rises.
options: Right: humidity caps evaporation just when it is the only route left.
Humidity slows evaporation; it does not add a cooling route.
Secreted sweat cools only when it evaporates; dripping sweat removes almost no heat.
Humid air does not make sweating start sooner; it makes each liter less effective.

questions.q: The air is 35 °C and the person starts walking steadily, doubling the heat made to about 150 kcal an hour. What must happen to evaporation?
options: It must rise to about 150 kcal/h
Nothing: the dry routes will carry the extra heat
It can stay at 75, because core temperature is regulated
It must fall, to save water

why.correct: At 35 °C the air is as warm as the skin, so radiation, conduction and convection carry nothing. For core temperature to hold steady, evaporation must remove all 150 kcal an hour: about a quarter of a liter of evaporated sweat each hour (150 ÷ 580).
options: Right: evaporation is the only route left, so it must match the heat made.
At 35 °C the dry routes remove nothing, however much heat is made.
Core temperature stays steady only if heat lost matches heat made; if evaporation stays at 75, heat builds up.
Sweating less would let heat build up; the water must be replaced by drinking.

graphs.title: Blood pH and PCO2 at a fixed bicarbonate
graphs.intro: Each line is the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = 6.1 + log(HCO3− ÷ (0.03 × PCO2)), drawn for one bicarbonate concentration. Moving along a line is a change in breathing; moving from one line to another is a change in bicarbonate.
graphs.alt: Blood pH against arterial PCO2 from 20 to 90 millimeters of mercury, with bicarbonate held at 24 millimoles per liter. The line falls as PCO2 rises: pH about 7.7 at 20, 7.4 at 40, 7.26 at 55 and 7.1 at 80. Dashed lines mark the normal pH range of 7.35 to 7.45.

questions.q: With bicarbonate at 24 mmol/L, read the pH at a normal PCO2 of 40 mm Hg.
questions.why: About 7.40. Dissolved carbon dioxide is 0.03 × 40 = 1.2 mmol/L, the ratio is 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20, and 6.1 + log 20 = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4.

questions.q: A sedative overdose doubles PCO2 to 80 mm Hg before the kidneys act. Read the pH.
questions.why: About 7.10. Doubling PCO2 halves the ratio, from 20 to 10, and halving the ratio lowers pH by 0.3.

questions.q: At what PCO2 does this line reach a pH of 7.30?
questions.why: About 50 mm Hg. A pH of 7.3 needs a ratio of about 16: 24 ÷ 16 = 1.5 mmol/L of dissolved carbon dioxide, and 1.5 ÷ 0.03 = 50 mm Hg.

questions.q: With bicarbonate held at 24 mmol/L, in which region does the pH fall below 7.35?
options: PCO2 above 45 mm Hg
Normal PCO2, 35 to 45 mm Hg
PCO2 below 35 mm Hg
Nowhere: pH depends only on bicarbonate

why.correct: Above about 45 mm Hg the line drops below 7.35. With bicarbonate unchanged, carbon dioxide retained by too little breathing is enough to make the blood acidic.
options: Right: a high PCO2 lowers the ratio below about 18.
In the normal range the ratio stays close to 20 and pH stays within 7.35 to 7.45.
A low PCO2 raises the ratio, so pH rises: this is where the blood becomes alkaline.
pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to carbon dioxide, so PCO2 matters as much as bicarbonate.

questions.q: A fixed acid uses up half the bicarbonate, leaving 12 mmol/L. How does the line change?
options: It shifts down by about 0.3 pH units at every PCO2
It shifts up by about 0.3 pH units at every PCO2
It gets steeper but still passes through 7.4 at a PCO2 of 40
It does not change, because PCO2 has not changed

why.correct: Halving bicarbonate halves the ratio at every PCO2, and halving the ratio lowers pH by 0.3. At a PCO2 of 40 the pH is now 7.10.
options: Right: the whole line drops by log 2, about 0.3.
Less bicarbonate lowers the ratio; the line moves down, not up.
Halving the top of the ratio changes pH by the same amount at every PCO2, so the line moves down without changing shape.
The line is drawn for one bicarbonate. A new bicarbonate means a new line, even at the same PCO2.

questions.q: On the 12 mmol/L line, the person now breathes harder and lowers PCO2 from 40 to 25 mm Hg. Where does the blood move?
options: Left along the 12 mmol/L line, with pH rising from 7.10 to about 7.30
Back onto the 24 mmol/L line at a pH of 7.40
Right along the 12 mmol/L line, with pH falling further
Straight up, because breathing adds bicarbonate

why.correct: Breathing changes PCO2, not bicarbonate, so the blood stays on the 12 mmol/L line. At 25 mm Hg the ratio is 12 ÷ 0.75 = 16, and pH is 7.30: better, but bicarbonate is still half normal.
options: Right: the lungs restore part of the ratio, not the bicarbonate.
Only the kidneys can replace the bicarbonate that the acid used up; breathing cannot put the blood back on the 24 line.
Breathing harder lowers PCO2, which is a move to the left, and pH rises.
Breathing removes carbon dioxide; it adds no bicarbonate.

graphs.title: Plasma potassium and the resting potential
graphs.intro: Schematic resting potential of a skeletal or heart muscle cell as plasma potassium changes, with threshold held at about −55 mV. The gap between the line and threshold is how far a cell must be pushed to fire. At low potassium, real cells fall short of this line, and at very low levels some even depolarize instead; read the line for direction, not exact values.
graphs.alt: Resting membrane potential in millivolts against plasma potassium from 2 to 8 millimoles per liter. The line rises from about −108 millivolts at 2 to −90 at 4 and about −72 at 8. A dashed line marks threshold at −55 millivolts.

questions.q: Read the resting potential at a normal plasma potassium of 4 mmol/L.
questions.why: About −90 mV, set mainly by potassium leaking out of the cell down its concentration gradient.

questions.q: At a plasma potassium of 7 mmol/L, how far is the resting potential from threshold?
questions.why: The line sits at about −75 mV and threshold at −55 mV, a gap of about 20 mV instead of the usual 35. More potassium outside means less leaks out, so the resting potential moves toward threshold.

questions.q: In which region is the cell hyperpolarized by hypokalemia?
options: Plasma potassium below 3.5 mmol/L
Plasma potassium from 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L
Plasma potassium above 5.0 mmol/L

why.correct: Below 3.5 mmol/L more potassium leaks out of cells, so the resting potential becomes more negative and skeletal muscle is harder to excite: weakness. Heart cells also repolarize more slowly, which causes arrhythmias.
options: Right: hypokalemia, below 3.5 mmol/L.
This is the normal range.
Above 5.0 is hyperkalemia, which moves the resting potential toward threshold, not away from it.

questions.q: A patient with a plasma potassium of 7 mmol/L is given calcium by vein. What changes on the graph?
options: The threshold line moves up (less negative), widening the gap
The patient’s point moves left, because calcium lowers potassium
The resting potential line moves down (more negative)
Nothing: calcium does not act on heart cells

why.correct: IV calcium raises the threshold of heart muscle cells, restoring the gap between rest and threshold and protecting the heart for 30 to 60 minutes. It does not lower potassium at all.
options: Right: calcium moves threshold, not potassium.
Calcium leaves plasma potassium where it is; insulin with glucose, binders and dialysis lower it.
The resting potential is set by potassium, which calcium does not change.
Calcium is the first treatment for dangerous hyperkalemia precisely because it acts on heart cells.

questions.q: Instead, insulin with glucose is given. Where does the patient’s point go over the next 30 minutes?
options: Left along the same line, toward a lower potassium and a more negative resting potential
Right along the line, toward threshold
The line itself shifts up
It stays put until the kidneys excrete potassium

why.correct: Insulin stimulates sodium–potassium pumps, moving potassium into cells. Plasma potassium falls, and the cell moves back along the same line, away from threshold. The body’s total potassium has not changed.
options: Right: a shift into cells lowers the plasma value within minutes.
Insulin lowers plasma potassium, a move to the left.
The line shows how the resting potential depends on potassium; insulin changes the potassium, not that relationship.
The ECF holds under 2% of body potassium, so moving some into cells lowers plasma potassium within minutes, before any is excreted.

graphs.title: ADH and thirst against plasma osmolality
graphs.intro: Plasma ADH as plasma osmolality changes, with blood volume normal. Values are schematic, shaped on studies of healthy adults: ADH starts to rise at about 280 to 285 mOsm/kg, and thirst switches on a little higher.
graphs.alt: Plasma ADH in picograms per milliliter against plasma osmolality from 270 to 310 milliosmoles per kilogram. ADH stays near 0.5 below about 282, then rises steadily: about 3.6 at 290, 7.6 at 300 and 11.6 at 310. A vertical line at about 293 marks where thirst switches on.

questions.q: Read the plasma ADH at an osmolality of 290 mOsm/kg.
questions.why: About 3.6 pg/mL. Near the set point there is always some ADH, so the kidneys can move urine concentration either way.

questions.q: At about what osmolality does ADH begin to rise above its baseline?
questions.why: About 280 to 285 mOsm/kg. Above that, each small rise in osmolality adds more ADH, which is why the osmoreceptors can correct a change of only 1 to 2%.

questions.q: In which range do your kidneys start saving water before you feel thirsty?
options: ADH rising, no thirst
ADH at baseline
ADH and thirst
Thirst always comes first

why.correct: ADH rises from about 282 mOsm/kg, but thirst switches on only near 293. So everyday rises are corrected by the kidneys saving water before you notice anything; thirst takes over for larger rises, and only drinking can replace water already lost.
options: Right: the ADH threshold is lower than the thirst threshold.
Here plasma is dilute and ADH is at its lowest, so the kidneys are passing extra water, not saving it.
By this range thirst has switched on too.
In most studies thirst switches on at a slightly higher osmolality than ADH starts to rise.

questions.q: After a person loses about 15% of her blood volume, how does the line change?
options: It shifts left and gets steeper: more ADH at every osmolality
It shifts right: less ADH at every osmolality
It flattens: ADH stops responding to osmolality
It does not change, because the line depends only on osmolality

why.correct: A fall in blood volume of more than about 5 to 10%, sensed by stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the atria and large vessels, adds its own drive to ADH release. The kidneys then keep water even when the plasma is normal or dilute: volume wins over concentration.
options: Right: volume loss lowers the threshold and raises the sensitivity.
Losing volume increases ADH release; it does not reduce it.
ADH still follows osmolality; volume loss adds to the drive.
ADH has a second trigger, a fall in blood volume, which moves the whole line.

questions.q: A man at 290 mOsm/kg drinks 2 L of water fast, and his osmolality falls to about 277 mOsm/kg. Where does he move on the graph?
options: Left along the line, to baseline ADH
Right along the line, to more ADH
Onto a new line shifted to the left
He stays at 290, because the kidneys correct it at once

why.correct: Drinking water lowers osmolality, a move to the left along the same line. Below about 282 ADH falls to baseline, the collecting ducts become nearly waterproof, and over the next hours the kidneys pass the extra water as dilute urine.
options: Right: lower osmolality, less ADH.
Water dilutes the plasma, lowering osmolality, which moves him left, not right.
His blood volume barely changes, so the line itself stays where it is; he moves along it.
The kidneys need hours to pass 2 L, so the osmolality does fall first.

graphs.title: Respiratory acidosis: the kidneys catch up
graphs.intro: A patient’s PaCO2 rises to 60 mm Hg and stays there. The three panels show her ABG over the next six days, as renal compensation raises bicarbonate. The pH values follow from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
graphs.alt: Three panels against time from 0 to 6 days. PaCO2 is flat at 60 millimeters of mercury. Bicarbonate is 26 millimoles per liter for the first half day, then rises to 28 at day 1, about 30 at day 3 and 31 by day 5. pH starts at 7.26 and rises to about 7.29 at day 1 and 7.34 by day 5, still below the 7.35 line.

questions.q: Read the pH at the start, when PaCO2 has just reached 60 mm Hg.
questions.why: About 7.26. Bicarbonate is still 26, so the ratio is 26 ÷ (0.03 × 60) = 14.4, and 6.1 + log 14.4 = 7.26: an uncompensated respiratory acidosis.

questions.q: Read the bicarbonate on day 5.
questions.why: About 31 mmol/L. Over 3 to 5 days, tubule cells exposed to the high PCO2 secrete more H+ and excrete more ammonium, adding new bicarbonate to the blood.

questions.q: During which period is this an uncompensated respiratory acidosis?
options: The first hours
Days 1 to 6
The whole six days
Never: the lungs compensate at once

why.correct: In the first hours PaCO2 is high but bicarbonate is still within 22 to 26 and pH is low, so the other system has not yet responded. Once bicarbonate rises above 26 while pH stays below 7.35, it is partially compensated.
options: Right: bicarbonate is still normal.
From about day 1 bicarbonate is above 26, so compensation is under way: partially compensated.
Bicarbonate leaves the normal range within the first day or so, so the label changes.
The lungs are the cause here; they cannot compensate for a problem they are causing. The kidneys do, slowly.

questions.q: Suppose her kidneys could not raise their H+ secretion, but otherwise kept working as before. How would the bicarbonate and pH panels differ?
options: Both would stay flat near their starting values: bicarbonate about 26, pH about 7.26
Bicarbonate would rise faster and pH would overshoot above 7.45
Bicarbonate would fall and pH would rise
Nothing would change, because the lungs would compensate instead

why.correct: Renal compensation needs the kidneys to secrete more H+, and time. Without that, no new bicarbonate is added, the ratio stays near 14 and pH stays near 7.26. (Kidneys that were failing outright would do worse: they could not excrete even the usual daily acid, so bicarbonate would drift down and pH fall further.)
options: Right: no renal compensation.
Compensation seldom overshoots, and kidneys that cannot raise H+ secretion add no extra bicarbonate at all.
Without a renal response no new bicarbonate is added, and the pH cannot rise without it.
The lungs are the source of the problem here, so they cannot compensate.

graphs.title: Hormones, follicle and endometrium across a 28-day cycle
graphs.intro: One 28-day model cycle, day 1 being the first day of bleeding. From the top: the pituitary hormones LH and FSH, the ovarian hormones estradiol and progesterone, and the thickness of the endometrium. The dashed line marks ovulation. Endometrium thickness is shown as measured on ultrasound, across both walls of the cavity. Values are typical, not from one woman; real cycles vary, mostly in the days before ovulation.
graphs.alt: Four stacked graphs over days 1 to 28 of a model cycle, with ovulation marked at day 14. Top: LH stays near 5 IU/L, rises steeply from about day 12 to a sharp peak of about 60 IU/L on day 13.5, and falls back to about 4 by day 17. FSH starts at about 7 to 8 IU/L, falls to about 4.5 by day 10, makes a smaller peak of about 12 at mid-cycle, stays near 3 in the second half and starts rising in the last days. Second: estradiol rises from about 40 pg/mL to a peak of about 285 on day 12.5, falls to about 100 by day 15, rises to a second, lower hump of about 165 around day 21 and falls to 50 by day 28. Third: progesterone stays below 1 ng/mL until ovulation, rises to about 14 around day 21 and falls below 1 by day 28. Bottom: endometrium thickness falls from about 9 mm to 3 mm during days 1 to 5, grows to about 10 mm by day 14 and about 13 mm by day 21, stays thick until about day 26 and thins over the last two days.

questions.q: Read the peak LH level.
questions.why: About 60 IU/L, on day 13.5: roughly twelve times the level of the early follicular phase. That is the LH surge, and ovulation follows about 34 to 36 hours after it begins.

questions.q: Read the highest estradiol level, and note when it comes compared with the LH peak.
questions.why: About 285 pg/mL, on day 12.5, a day before LH peaks. Estradiol peaks as the LH surge begins and then falls, because LH is already turning the follicle’s cells toward making progesterone.

questions.q: On about which day does progesterone peak?
questions.why: Around day 21, about a week after ovulation, when the corpus luteum is fully formed. That mid-luteal week is also when the lining is ready for an embryo to attach.

questions.q: During which stretch is estradiol’s feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary positive rather than negative?
options: Days 11 to 13.5, while estradiol stays above about 200 pg/mL
Days 1 to 5, while estradiol is lowest
Days 5 to 10, while FSH is falling and estradiol climbs
Days 18 to 24, when estradiol rises to its second, lower hump

why.correct: When estradiol from the dominant follicle stays high, above roughly 200 pg/mL for about two days, it switches from brake to accelerator: GnRH output rises and each pulse releases far more LH. LH starts shooting up in the second half of this stretch and peaks at its end, on day 13.5.
options: Right: high, sustained estradiol drives the surge.
Early in the cycle estradiol is low and FSH is rising because the brake has lifted; there is no positive feedback.
Here estradiol and inhibin are rising but still moderate, and they hold FSH down by ordinary negative feedback.
In the luteal phase, progesterone is high, and with it estradiol gives the strongest negative feedback of the cycle; LH stays at its lowest.

questions.q: FSH falls during which stretch, and what does that fall do in the ovary?
options: Days 5 to 10: estradiol and inhibin lower it, so one follicle is selected
Days 1 to 5: the period washes FSH out of the blood
Days 14 to 18: progesterone lowers FSH, and that is when the dominant follicle is chosen
Days 25 to 28: the corpus luteum makes FSH fall, and all the follicles die

why.correct: The follicles rescued at the start of the cycle release estradiol and inhibin, which feed back negatively. As FSH falls, the follicle with the most FSH receptor proteins keeps growing and the rest undergo atresia: negative feedback selects one follicle.
options: Right: negative feedback selects the dominant follicle.
Bleeding does not remove FSH. FSH is high at the start because the corpus luteum’s brake has just lifted.
By day 14 the dominant follicle has already been chosen and has ovulated.
At the end of the cycle FSH is rising, because the dying corpus luteum’s hormones are falling.

questions.q: During which phase does the functional layer grow fastest, and which hormone drives it?
options: The proliferative phase, driven by estradiol
The secretory phase, driven by rising progesterone
The menstrual phase, driven by falling progesterone
The proliferative phase, driven by LH

why.correct: From about day 5 to day 14, estradiol from the growing follicles makes the basal layer’s cells divide and rebuild the functional layer, which thickens several-fold by ovulation.
options: Right: estradiol builds.
Progesterone changes the thick lining, coiling its glands and arteries, without adding much more thickness.
Falling progesterone sheds the functional layer; the lining is thinnest then.
LH acts on the ovary, not on the endometrium.

questions.q: In the last days of the cycle, which change in the ovary starts both the next period and the next rise in FSH?
options: The corpus luteum dies, and its hormones fall
A new dominant follicle releases a burst of estradiol
LH surges a second time, late in the cycle
The endometrium stops making its own progesterone

why.correct: Without a pregnancy the corpus luteum dies after 12 to 14 days. Falling progesterone sets off breakdown of the functional layer, and the loss of its brake lets FSH climb, rescuing the next group of follicles.
options: Right: one event, two results.
No follicle can become dominant while the corpus luteum’s hormones hold FSH and LH down.
There is one LH surge per cycle; in the late luteal phase LH is at its lowest.
The endometrium does not make progesterone; the corpus luteum does.

questions.q: She takes the combined pill every day this month. How does the LH curve change?
options: It stays low all month, with no mid-cycle peak
The peak comes earlier, on about day 7
The peak is taller, because the pill contains estrogen
It is unchanged; the pill acts only on the uterus

why.correct: Steady synthetic estrogen and progestin keep negative feedback on all month. FSH stays low, no follicle becomes dominant, estradiol never stays high for two days, and positive feedback never starts: no surge, no ovulation.
options: Right: no surge.
A surge needs high estradiol from a dominant follicle; the pill prevents one from forming at any time.
The pill’s estrogen is steady and paired with a progestin, which keeps feedback negative. It removes the peak rather than enlarging it.
Preventing the surge in the pituitary is the pill’s main action; the effects on mucus and lining are backups.

questions.q: In a woman whose cycles are 32 days long, how does the LH peak shift, and what happens to the phase after it?
options: About 4 days later; the phase after ovulation stays about 14 days
It stays at day 14, and the phase after ovulation stretches to 18 days
It moves 2 days later, and the phases before and after ovulation each gain 2 days
It moves earlier, because her follicles grow faster

why.correct: The luteal phase is set by the corpus luteum’s lifespan, about 12 to 14 days, so the extra days fall before ovulation. Ovulation day ≈ cycle length − 14 = 32 − 14 = day 18, and the surge moves with it.
options: Right: the follicular phase absorbs the difference.
The phase after ovulation is the steady one; a longer cycle lengthens the phase before ovulation.
The variation is not split evenly; most of it is in the follicular phase, while the luteal phase stays about 12 to 14 days.
A longer cycle means the dominant follicle takes longer to be selected and grow, so ovulation comes later, not earlier.

questions.q: After both ovaries are removed, how do the FSH and LH curves change?
options: Both rise and stay high, with no cycle
Both fall to zero, because the ovaries made them
FSH rises but LH falls
Both stay the same; the pituitary runs on its own

why.correct: FSH and LH come from the pituitary, not the ovaries. With no estradiol, progesterone or inhibin to brake them, both rise and stay high, FSH most of all because it has lost both estradiol and inhibin, the same pattern as after menopause.
options: Right: the brakes are gone.
The ovaries are the target of FSH and LH, not their source.
LH also loses its brake, estradiol and progesterone, so it rises too.
The pituitary’s output depends on feedback from the ovaries; without it the levels climb.

graphs.title: FSH and the selection of one follicle
graphs.intro: Early in each cycle a group of follicles starts to grow while FSH is high. Ultrasound can follow their size. This graph follows FSH and the diameters of two follicles, the one that becomes dominant and one of the others, from the first day of bleeding. Values are typical.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over days 1 to 13 of a cycle. Top: FSH rises from about 7 IU/L on day 1 to 8 on day 3, then falls steadily to about 4.5 by days 10 to 12. Bottom: both follicles are about 4 mm on day 1 and grow alike to about 9 mm by day 7. After that the dominant follicle keeps growing, about 1.5 mm a day, to about 19 mm on day 13, while the other stops at about 9.5 mm on day 8 and shrinks to about 5 mm by day 13.

questions.q: Read the dominant follicle’s diameter on day 13.
questions.why: About 19 mm. It grows about 1.5 mm a day in the second week and reaches about 2 cm when mature, bulging from the ovary’s surface.

questions.q: Read the highest FSH level on the graph.
questions.why: About 8 IU/L, on day 3. FSH is highest at the start of the cycle, which is when the group of follicles that happen to be ready is rescued from atresia.

questions.q: During which days do the two follicles’ paths split, and why then?
options: Days 6 to 9, as FSH falls and only the most sensitive one keeps up
Days 1 to 5, as FSH rises and the highest FSH picks out one follicle
Days 9 to 13, when the dominant follicle stops needing FSH altogether
They never split; both follicles are released

why.correct: Estradiol and inhibin from the growing group lower FSH. The follicle with the most FSH receptor proteins and the best blood supply keeps growing on less FSH, and it gains LH receptor proteins; the others lose their FSH support.
options: Right: falling FSH selects one.
Rising FSH rescues the whole group; selection comes when FSH falls.
By then selection is over. The dominant follicle can keep growing on low FSH because it is the most sensitive to FSH and also responds to LH.
Only the dominant follicle usually reaches the mature stage; the other shrinks.

questions.q: What is happening to the other follicle from day 9 on?
options: Atresia: it degenerates and never opens
It becomes a corpus luteum
It rests and will be released next month
It merges with the dominant follicle

why.correct: Without enough FSH, the follicle’s cells die and it degenerates. Atresia is the fate of more than 99% of follicles, and it, not ovulation, is what empties the ovary over a lifetime.
options: Right: atresia.
A corpus luteum forms only from a follicle that has released its oocyte.
A follicle that has lost its FSH support dies; it does not wait for another month.
Each follicle is a separate oocyte with its own cells; they do not merge.

questions.q: In fertility treatment, daily FSH injections keep FSH high from day 3 on. How does the other follicle’s curve change?
options: It keeps growing alongside the dominant one
It shrinks sooner
It is unchanged, because selection is fixed by day 1
It becomes the only follicle to grow, and the dominant one shrinks

why.correct: Selection depends on FSH falling. If FSH stays high, the other follicles keep their support, avoid atresia and keep growing, so several mature together. That is how clinics collect several oocytes in one cycle.
options: Right: high FSH rescues the others.
More FSH supports follicles; it does not speed their death.
Which follicles survive depends on FSH over the following days, so keeping it high changes the outcome.
Extra FSH supports every ready follicle; it does not turn off the most sensitive one.

graphs.title: Follicles left in the ovaries across life
graphs.intro: The number of follicles left in both ovaries together, from birth to 55. No new follicles are made after birth, so the curve can only fall. Values are typical; the numbers vary widely between women.
graphs.alt: A single falling curve. At birth about 1.5 million follicles (1,500 thousand) remain. The count falls steeply through childhood, to about 800 thousand at age 5 and about 350 thousand at puberty around 13, then more slowly: about 160 thousand at 25, 60 thousand at 35, 15 thousand at 40, and about 1 thousand at 51, the average age of menopause.

questions.q: About how many follicles remain at puberty, in thousands?
questions.why: About 350 thousand, roughly 300,000 to 400,000, all holding primary oocytes still paused in prophase I.

questions.q: About how many follicles, in thousands, are lost between birth and puberty?
questions.why: About 1,500 − 350 = 1,150 thousand, over a million follicles, lost before a single one has been ovulated. They die by atresia.

questions.q: Only about 400 oocytes are released in a lifetime. Across the whole curve, what removes almost all the others?
options: Atresia, the death of follicles that lose their support
Ovulation, about ten follicles a month
Menstruation, which sheds follicles with the lining
The formation of new follicles to replace old ones

why.correct: More than 99% of follicles undergo atresia, most of them before puberty and the rest in the groups that start growing each month but are not selected.
options: Right: atresia empties the ovary.
Only one follicle usually ovulates each month, about 400 in a lifetime, a tiny share of the fall.
Menstruation sheds the endometrium’s functional layer, not anything from the ovary.
No new follicles are made after birth; the curve only falls.

questions.q: In which stretch do cycles become irregular and then stop, and why?
options: From about 45: too few follicles are left to answer FSH
From about 13 to 20, because the follicles are not yet mature enough
From about 25 to 35: the fall is steepest
At birth: the oocytes are paused

why.correct: As the last follicles are used up, fewer grow each month, so less inhibin and estradiol are made. FSH rises first and most, ovulation fails more often, and when no follicle responds, periods stop for good.
options: Right: the supply runs out.
Early cycles can be irregular because the LH surge takes a year or more to mature, but that is not a shortage of follicles.
The steepest fall in numbers is in childhood, and cycles are regular through these years.
Cycles begin only at puberty.

questions.q: At 30, a woman has chemotherapy that destroys about nine tenths of her remaining follicles. How does her curve change?
options: It drops at 30 and reaches the menopause level years earlier than usual
It rises again after treatment as new follicles form
It is unchanged, because only growing follicles are harmed
It drops at 30 but her menopause comes at the usual age

why.correct: No follicles are made after birth, so a lost supply cannot be replaced. Starting from about a tenth of the usual number, she reaches the level of about a thousand follicles years sooner, and menopause comes early.
options: Right: an early menopause.
The oogonia that made follicles are gone by birth.
This treatment is described as destroying resting follicles too, so the count falls.
Menopause follows when the follicles run out, so a smaller supply runs out sooner.

graphs.title: hCG, progesterone, estrogens and hPL across pregnancy
graphs.intro: Four hormones of pregnancy, each drawn as a percent of its own highest level in a typical pregnancy, since their actual amounts differ a thousandfold. Weeks are counted from the first day of the last menstrual period. The numbers are typical, not from one woman.
graphs.alt: A line graph of four hormones against weeks of pregnancy from 0 to 40, each as a percent of its own peak. hCG rises from about week 4, peaks at 100% at week 10, falls to about 20% by week 18 and stays near 15 to 18% to the end. Progesterone starts near 10%, stays nearly flat until week 10, then climbs steadily to 100% at week 40. Estrogens start near zero and climb, more and more steeply, to 100% at week 40. hPL starts near zero at week 4 and rises steadily to a peak near week 38. A shaded band from week 7 to 9 marks where the main source of progesterone shifts from the corpus luteum to the placenta.

y.label: Level, share of its own peak

questions.q: At about which week of pregnancy does hCG peak?
questions.why: About week 10 on the clinical count, which is about 7 to 8 weeks after fertilization. Until then hCG roughly doubles every two to three days.

questions.q: Read hCG at week 24, as a percent of its peak.
questions.why: About 15%. After its peak hCG falls to a low plateau for the rest of pregnancy. Why it falls is not fully known, but the fall does no harm: by then the placenta makes enough progesterone itself.

questions.q: During which weeks does the main source of progesterone shift from the corpus luteum to the placenta?
options: Weeks 7 to 9
Weeks 3 to 5
Weeks 16 to 20
Weeks 36 to 40

why.correct: From about weeks 7 to 9 the placenta takes over progesterone production. Removing the corpus luteum before about week 7 ends the pregnancy unless progesterone is given; from about week 9, it does no harm.
options: Right: the shaded band.
In weeks 3 to 5 the embryo is only just implanting, and the corpus luteum, rescued by hCG, is the only real source.
By weeks 16 to 20 the takeover is long finished; progesterone is already climbing on the placenta’s output.
At the end of pregnancy the placenta has been the source for months; progesterone stays high right up to delivery.

questions.q: Around when does a home urine pregnancy test usually first turn positive?
options: About week 4, around the day the period is due
About week 10, when hCG reaches its highest level of the pregnancy
About week 1, the first day of the last period
About week 20, when hPL is halfway to its peak

why.correct: hCG enters the mother’s blood 8 to 10 days after fertilization and spills into her urine. By the day her period is due, week 4 on the clinical count, there is usually enough to detect, although it is still a tiny share of its later peak.
options: Right: the test turns positive long before the peak.
The test does not wait for the peak; it detects hCG while it is still low and doubling.
Week 1 is before ovulation, so there is no embryo and no hCG yet.
hPL is not what the test detects; the test uses antibodies against the part unique to hCG.

questions.q: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy are usually worst in weeks 9 to 12. Which hormone curve peaks in that stretch?
options: hCG
Progesterone
Estrogens
hPL

why.correct: Nausea peaks with hCG around weeks 9 to 12. A placental hormone that acts on the brainstem’s vomiting area, GDF15, is now thought to be a main driver, and it rises over the same weeks.
options: Right: hCG peaks at week 10.
Progesterone is still low and climbing slowly at weeks 9 to 12; it keeps rising long after nausea fades.
Estrogens are near their lowest in these weeks and highest at term, when nausea has usually gone.
hPL is only about a tenth of its peak at week 12 and rises steadily after that.

questions.q: In a pregnancy with placental insufficiency, the placenta, and its syncytiotrophoblast, is much smaller than usual. How does the hPL curve change?
options: It rises less and ends well below the usual peak
It rises higher, to make up for the small placenta
It peaks earlier, at week 10, like hCG
It does not change, because the pituitary makes hPL

why.correct: The syncytiotrophoblast makes hPL in proportion to its own mass, which is why hPL climbs as the placenta grows. A small placenta makes less, so hPL runs lower, one reason a low hPL can signal a failing placenta.
options: Right: less syncytiotrophoblast, less hPL.
hPL is not regulated upward to match the fetus’s needs; its output follows the amount of placental tissue.
The shape follows placental growth, which continues to late pregnancy; only hCG peaks early.
hPL is made by the placenta, not the pituitary.

questions.q: A fetus’s adrenal cortex barely works, while the placenta is healthy. How does the estrogen curve change?
options: It stays far lower, because the placenta lacks the fetal androgen it converts
It rises higher, because the placenta makes estrogens from cholesterol by itself
It is unchanged, because the mother’s ovaries make these estrogens
It falls to zero only after birth

why.correct: The placenta lacks the enzymes to build estrogens from cholesterol, so it converts an androgen made by the fetal adrenal cortex. Without that supply, estrogen output, mostly estriol, stays low: the placenta and fetus make estrogens together.
options: Right: no fetal androgen, little estrogen.
The placenta cannot build estrogens from cholesterol alone; that is exactly why it depends on the fetal androgen.
In pregnancy nearly all the estrogen comes from the placenta, not the mother’s ovaries.
The fall at birth follows delivery of the placenta; this change is present all through pregnancy.

questions.q: In an ectopic pregnancy implanted in a uterine tube, how does the early hCG curve usually differ from a healthy pregnancy’s?
options: It rises more slowly than the usual doubling every two to three days
It rises faster and peaks earlier
It is exactly the same as a healthy pregnancy’s until the tube ruptures
hCG is absent, so a urine pregnancy test stays negative throughout

why.correct: The trophoblast in a thin tube wall cannot grow and secrete as it would in the endometrium, so hCG often rises more slowly than the usual doubling. A positive test with a slow rise, one-sided pain and no pregnancy seen in the uterus points to an ectopic pregnancy.
options: Right: a slow rise is a warning sign.
A faster rise is not the typical pattern of an ectopic pregnancy.
The rise usually differs well before rupture, which is why serial hCG levels help find it early.
The trophoblast still makes hCG, so the test is positive.

graphs.title: Fetal weight from week 20 to birth
graphs.intro: Typical (median) fetal weight in the second half of pregnancy, from ultrasound-based growth charts, in weeks from the last menstrual period. Real babies vary widely around these values.
graphs.alt: A line graph of fetal weight in grams against weeks of pregnancy from 20 to 40. Weight rises slowly at first and then faster: about 330 g at week 20, 670 g at week 24, about 1,200 g at week 28, about 1,950 g at week 32, about 2,800 g at week 36 and about 3,600 g at week 40. Shaded bands mark the edge of viability at weeks 22 to 24 and term from week 37.

questions.q: Read the typical fetal weight at 28 weeks.
questions.why: About 1.2 kg. The notes put the fetus at about 1 kg around weeks 26 to 28, when the eyes open.

questions.q: Read the weights at 34 and 36 weeks. About how many grams a week is the fetus gaining between them?
questions.why: About 2,380 g at 34 weeks and 2,810 g at 36: roughly 430 g in two weeks, about 220 g a week. At week 20 the whole fetus weighs only about one and a half times that.

questions.q: In which stretch can a baby born early first sometimes survive with intensive care?
options: Weeks 22 to 24
Weeks 20 to 21
Weeks 30 to 32
Weeks 37 to 40, at term

why.correct: Around weeks 22 to 24 the lungs reach the stage where gas exchange first becomes barely possible: the edge of viability. The baby weighs only about 500 to 700 g.
options: Right: the lungs set the limit.
Before about week 22 the capillaries have not yet grown close enough to the airway lining, so the lungs cannot exchange gas.
Most babies born at 30 to 32 weeks survive; viability begins much earlier.
Weeks 37 to 40 are term, not the edge of viability.

questions.q: In which stretch does the fetus gain the most grams per week, and what builds up in its body then?
options: The last 8 weeks: fat, including brown fat, under the skin
Weeks 20 to 24: new organs still being formed from the germ layers
Weeks 20 to 24: bone
It gains the same number of grams every week

why.correct: The curve is steepest from about week 32 on. Most of the grams are still lean tissue and water, but fat now builds up under the skin and fills out the wrinkled skin, and brown fat is laid down for keeping warm after birth.
options: Right: the steepest stretch, when fat builds up.
Every organ system is present by about week 10; the fetal period is growth and maturation, not new organs.
Bones ossify and grow throughout, but the steepest gain in grams is late, not at 20 to 24 weeks.
The weekly gain grows from about 75 g at week 20 to over 200 g in the last weeks, so the grams per week are far from equal.

questions.q: From about week 28, the placenta can no longer keep up. How does the growth curve change?
options: It flattens after week 28 and ends well below the typical weight
It rises more steeply, because the fetus takes more from the mother
It drops below 1,000 g as the fetus loses weight
It is unchanged until birth

why.correct: Everything the fetus builds with crosses the placenta. With less oxygen and glucose crossing, growth slows but continues: the curve bends away from the typical one and the baby is born small, often with too little amniotic fluid.
options: Right: growth slows and the baby is small.
The fetus cannot take more than the placenta delivers; less supply means slower growth.
The fetus keeps growing, just more slowly; it does not usually lose weight.
The fall in supply shows in the growth curve within weeks.

questions.q: A mother has poorly controlled gestational diabetes in the second half of pregnancy. How does the growth curve change?
options: It rises more steeply and ends above the typical weight
It flattens, because the mother’s insulin blocks fetal growth
It is unchanged, because the placenta blocks the extra glucose
It peaks at 30 weeks and then falls

why.correct: Glucose crosses the placenta but the mother’s insulin does not, so the fetus secretes more insulin of its own, and fetal insulin drives growth. The baby grows large, which makes the shoulders more likely to get stuck.
options: Right: extra glucose plus fetal insulin means faster growth.
The mother’s insulin does not cross the placenta at all.
Glucose crosses the placenta freely by facilitated diffusion, down its gradient.
The extra growth continues to term; the curve does not turn down.

graphs.title: The mother’s circulation across pregnancy
graphs.intro: Top: heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output and total peripheral resistance, each as a percent change from the woman’s own value before pregnancy. Bottom: her mean arterial pressure, starting from 90 mm Hg. Weeks are counted from the last menstrual period. The curves are schematic but within the ranges measured in healthy pregnancies.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over weeks 0 to 40 of pregnancy. Top, percent change from before pregnancy: heart rate rises first, from week 4, reaching about +15% at week 20 and +22% at term. Stroke volume starts rising around week 8, reaches about +24% by weeks 24 to 28, and eases to about +18% at term. Cardiac output rises to about +40% by week 20 and +45 to 48% by weeks 24 to 32, easing slightly to +44% at term. Total peripheral resistance falls to about −30% by week 16 and about −35% at week 24, then eases to about −31% at term. Bottom: mean arterial pressure dips from 90 to about 83 mm Hg at week 20 and returns to about 90 by week 36.

questions.q: Read the rise in cardiac output at 24 weeks, as a percent of her value before pregnancy.
questions.why: About +45%: from about 5 L/min to about 7 L/min. Most of the rise in cardiac output has happened by weeks 20 to 24.

questions.q: Read her lowest mean arterial pressure.
questions.why: About 83 mm Hg, around week 20, some 7 mm Hg below her usual 90. Resistance has fallen by a third while cardiac output has risen by about 40%, and the fall in resistance wins slightly.

questions.q: Which rises first in early pregnancy, and in which weeks does it rise alone?
options: Heart rate, in about weeks 4 to 7
Stroke volume, in about weeks 4 to 7
Mean arterial pressure, in weeks 0 to 3
Peripheral resistance, in weeks 14 to 24

why.correct: Heart rate rises within the first weeks. Stroke volume follows a few weeks later, as the growing blood volume raises venous return and preload.
options: Right: the rate leads, the stroke volume follows.
Stroke volume waits for the blood volume to grow, so it lags heart rate by a few weeks.
Mean arterial pressure does not rise early; it dips in mid-pregnancy.
Resistance falls; it never rises in a healthy pregnancy.

questions.q: When is her blood pressure lowest, and why does it not rise with the cardiac output?
options: Weeks 14 to 24: the fall in resistance outweighs the output rise
Weeks 32 to 40: the heart has tired
Weeks 0 to 3: she has lost blood volume
Weeks 24 to 40: resistance rises above its value before pregnancy

why.correct: Mean arterial pressure is cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. Progesterone and nitric oxide relax the arterioles, and the placenta adds a low-resistance bed, so resistance falls about as much as output rises. The product, 1.40 × 0.66 ≈ 0.92 at week 20, dips below 1, most in mid-pregnancy.
options: Right: the fall in resistance slightly outweighs the rise in output.
Late in pregnancy the pressure returns toward her usual level; it is not at its lowest then.
Blood volume rises, not falls, from the first weeks.
Resistance stays below her value before pregnancy to the end, only easing a little.

questions.q: She develops preeclampsia at 34 weeks. How does the mean arterial pressure curve change?
options: It climbs well above her value before pregnancy
It falls further, because her plasma volume falls
It is unchanged, because her cardiac output does not change
It dips to 70 mm Hg, because her capillaries leak

why.correct: Damaged endothelium lets her arterioles constrict, so total peripheral resistance rises instead of staying low, and pressure climbs to 140/90 mm Hg or more (a mean above about 105).
options: Right: resistance rises, so pressure rises.
Her plasma volume does fall as capillaries leak, but the rise in resistance dominates, so pressure goes up.
Pressure depends on resistance too, and resistance rises sharply.
Leaky capillaries cause edema, but constricted arterioles raise the pressure.

graphs.title: Trisomy 21 and the mother’s age
graphs.intro: Births with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) per 1,000 births, by the mother’s age at delivery. Values are approximate population figures.
graphs.alt: A line graph of trisomy 21 births per 1,000 against the mother’s age from 20 to 45. The risk stays below about 1 per 1,000 from 20 to 25, rises slowly to about 1.1 at 30, then climbs faster: about 2.9 at 35, 5.7 at 38, 10 at 40, 18 at 42 and 33 at 45.

questions.q: Read the rate at a maternal age of 40, per 1,000 births.
questions.why: About 10 per 1,000, or 1 in 100, compared with about 1 in 1,200 at 25.

questions.q: Read the rate at a maternal age of 45, per 1,000 births.
questions.why: About 33 per 1,000, or 1 in 30: about 40 times the rate at 25.

questions.q: Over which ages does the rate climb most steeply, and what causes the rise?
options: From about 35 on: the oocyte’s chromosome links, never replaced, have weakened
From 20 to 30: the oocytes are too young to divide properly
From 30 to 35 only: then it levels off
It climbs evenly at every age, because every cell in the body ages at the same steady rate

why.correct: An oocyte pauses in meiosis I from before the mother’s birth until ovulation. The proteins holding its paired chromosomes together are not replaced, so after about 35 years they fail more and more often, and nondisjunction climbs.
options: Right: long pause, weak links.
The rate is lowest in the twenties; the oocytes’ links are still strong.
The rise keeps accelerating past 35; it does not level off.
The curve is flat early and steep late, because the damage builds up with the length of the pause.

questions.q: About 4% of Down syndrome comes from a translocation. How would a curve for the translocation form alone look?
options: Low and flat: its rate does not depend on the mother’s age
The same shape, just lower, still rising steeply once the mother passes 35
Falling with age
Rising steeply from age 20

why.correct: In the translocation form, most of an extra chromosome 21 is attached to another chromosome; in about a quarter of cases this is inherited from a parent who carries the rearrangement. It does not come from nondisjunction during the long pause in meiosis I, so it does not depend on the mother’s age.
options: Right: flat, because it has nothing to do with the pause.
Only nondisjunction rises with age; the translocation form has a different cause.
Nothing about a rearrangement makes it less likely with age.
A carrier parent can pass it on at any age, so the rate does not climb.

graphs.title: Reserve with age
graphs.intro: A schematic of an organ system’s maximal capacity, as a percent of its peak, across adult life. The lower dashed line is the capacity needed at rest; the upper one is what a major stress, such as pneumonia, needs. The shape is typical of many systems; real rates vary widely and are slower with regular exercise.
graphs.alt: A line graph of maximal capacity, as a percent of peak, against age from 20 to 90. Capacity stays at 100% until 30, then falls slowly and then faster: about 93% at 40, 84% at 50, 75% at 60, 66% at 70, 60% at 75, 55% at 80 and 44% at 90. A dashed line at 25% is the capacity needed at rest; capacity stays above it throughout. A dashed line at 60% is the capacity a major stress needs; capacity falls below it at about 75.

questions.q: Read the maximal capacity at 80.
questions.why: About 55% of peak. That is still more than twice what rest needs, so resting values are normal, but it is below what a major stress needs.

questions.q: At about what age does capacity fall below what a major stress needs?
questions.why: At about 75, where the curve crosses the 60% line. After that, a stress a younger body would absorb, such as influenza or pneumonia, can overwhelm the system even though everything looks normal at rest.

questions.q: In which stretch are resting values normal, yet a major stress cannot be met? What is that narrowing called?
options: From about 75 on: homeostenosis, the loss of reserve
From 20 to 30: homeostasis at its peak
From 30 to 75: disease replacing normal aging
Only after 90, when resting needs can no longer be met

why.correct: Capacity is above the resting line but below the stress line. Resting homeostasis is kept; the range over which a variable can be held steady has narrowed. That is homeostenosis, the story of Mrs. Castillo’s influenza.
options: Right: rest is met, stress is not.
At 20 to 30 capacity is at its peak and meets both needs easily.
The slow decline is normal aging, not disease; diseases are separate processes.
On this graph capacity stays above the resting line to 90; the loss of reserve shows well before resting needs fail.

questions.q: Over which ages is capacity at its peak on this graph?
options: From 20 to about 30
From 30 to 50
From 60 to 75
Capacity is highest at 90

why.correct: Many capacities, such as bone mass and muscle strength, peak around age 30 and decline after that.
options: Right: the plateau before the decline.
By 30 to 50 capacity is already falling, slowly at first.
By 60 to 75 capacity has fallen by a quarter to a third.
Capacity is lowest at 90 on this graph.

questions.q: She exercises regularly from middle age, aerobic and resistance training. How does her capacity curve change?
options: It stays higher and crosses the stress line much later
It rises above 100% of her youthful peak and stays there
It is unchanged, because aging sets the rate
It falls faster, because exercise wears the body out

why.correct: Much of the decline once blamed on age comes from inactivity. Exercise keeps the highest oxygen uptake, muscle and bone well above those of inactive peers at any age, so reserve lasts longer.
options: Right: the same shape, higher and later.
Exercise slows the decline; it does not stop aging or push capacity above its peak for decades.
Rates of decline vary widely, and inactivity speeds them; exercise changes the curve.
Regular exercise preserves capacity; resistance training even reverses much muscle loss.

questions.q: He smokes and is inactive from middle age. How does his curve change?
options: It falls faster and crosses the stress line years earlier
It is unchanged until he is ill
It rises, because the body adapts to smoking
It falls faster, but it never crosses the stress line because smoking spares reserve

why.correct: Inactivity lets muscle, bone and cardiac reserve fall faster, and smoking damages lungs and vessels on top of that. The curve drops below the stress line about a decade sooner, so ordinary illnesses become dangerous earlier.
options: Right: faster decline, earlier crossing.
The loss of reserve shows long before illness, as a shrinking gap between rest and maximum.
Smoking harms tissues; it does not build reserve.
A faster fall reaches the stress line earlier, not never.

graphs.title: How far the insertion sits from the elbow sets the pull
graphs.intro: You hold a 40-newton weight (about 4 kg) in your hand, 32 cm from the elbow, with the elbow bent at a right angle. The curve shows how hard the elbow-bending muscle must pull to hold it, depending on how far from the elbow its insertion sits. Each point comes from the balance rule: effort × effort arm = load × load arm. The weight of the forearm itself is ignored.
graphs.alt: A falling curve of the muscle pull needed, from 0 to 900 newtons, against the insertion’s distance from the elbow, from 3 to 12 cm. The pull is about 427 N at 3 cm, 320 N at 4 cm, 256 N at 5 cm, 160 N at 8 cm and 107 N at 12 cm. A dashed line at 40 N marks the weight itself; the curve stays far above it everywhere.

x.label: Insertion distance from the elbow (effort arm)

questions.q: Read the pull needed when the insertion is 4 cm from the elbow.
questions.why: About 320 N. Balance: effort × 4 cm = 40 N × 32 cm = 1,280 N·cm, so effort = 320 N, eight times the weight. That is the worked example in the notes.

questions.q: Read the pull needed when the insertion is 8 cm from the elbow.
questions.why: About 160 N. Doubling the effort arm from 4 to 8 cm halves the pull, because effort × effort arm must still equal the same 1,280 N·cm.

questions.q: Over which stretch of insertion distances must the muscle pull more than eight times the weight?
options: From 3 to 4 cm
From 8 to 12 cm
Nowhere on this graph
Everywhere on this graph

why.correct: Mechanical advantage is effort arm ÷ load arm. At 4 cm it is 4 ÷ 32 = 0.125, so the pull is exactly 8 times the weight; any closer and the ratio is smaller, so the pull is even larger.
options: Right: the closer the insertion, the smaller the mechanical advantage and the harder the pull.
Out at 8 to 12 cm the effort arm is longer, so the pull falls to 4 times the weight or less.
At 3 cm the pull is about 427 N, more than ten times the 40 N weight.
At 12 cm the pull is about 107 N, under three times the weight.

questions.q: Everywhere on this curve the pull is larger than the weight. Why, and what lever class is this?
options: Third-class: the effort arm is shorter than the load arm
Second-class: the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort
First-class: the elbow sits between the effort and the load
The muscle is weak, whatever the lever arrangement

why.correct: The insertion lies between the elbow (fulcrum) and the hand (load), so the effort is in the middle. Every insertion shown is closer than 32 cm, so the effort arm is shorter than the load arm and the muscle must out-pull the load.
options: Right: in a third-class lever the effort arm is always the shorter one, trading force for speed and range.
In a second-class lever the effort arm is always longer, so the pull would be smaller than the load.
Straightening the elbow is the first-class example; bending it puts the effort between fulcrum and load.
The large pull comes from the lever geometry, not from weakness. The same muscle moves the hand fast and far in return.

questions.q: You now hold an 80-newton weight in the same hand position. How does the curve change?
options: Every point doubles, so the curve moves up
Every point halves, so the curve moves down
The curve does not change, since the lever is the same
The curve moves right but keeps the same height

why.correct: Effort = load × load arm ÷ effort arm. Doubling the load doubles the right side of the balance at every insertion distance, so the whole curve doubles: 640 N at 4 cm.
options: Right: the pull is proportional to the load.
Halving would follow from a lighter load or a shorter load arm, not a heavier weight.
The lever sets the ratio between pull and load; a heavier load at the same ratio needs a proportionally larger pull.
The insertion distances have not changed, so the curve cannot slide sideways; it stretches upward.

questions.q: You keep the 40-newton weight but hold it 16 cm from the elbow, by resting it on your forearm. How does the curve change?
options: Every point halves, so the curve moves down
Every point doubles, so the curve moves up
Only the dashed weight line moves, down to 20 N
The curve does not change

why.correct: The load arm has halved, so load × load arm halves (640 N·cm instead of 1,280), and so does the pull at every insertion distance: 160 N at 4 cm. That is why you carry heavy things close to your elbow or body.
options: Right: a shorter load arm means a smaller pull for the same weight.
Doubling would need a heavier load or a longer load arm.
The weight is still 40 N, so its line stays; what changes is how much turning effect it has about the elbow.
Moving the load changes the load arm, and the pull depends on it directly.

graphs.title: Pressure in a leg compartment after a fracture
graphs.intro: An illustrative case: the pressure inside the anterior compartment of the leg in the hours after a tibia fracture, until a surgeon slits the fascia open at 6.5 hours. The numbers are typical, not from one patient. Current guidelines judge mainly from the signs, above all pain out of proportion to the injury. When the pressure is measured, they compare it with the lower number of the blood pressure: danger when the gap between them falls below about 30 mmHg. With a lower number of about 70 mmHg, that is a compartment pressure of about 40 mmHg. The graph uses 30 mmHg, a common working danger level.
graphs.alt: Compartment pressure in mmHg, from 0 to 100, over 10 hours. It starts at about 8 mmHg, climbs steadily to about 30 mmHg at 4 hours and about 44 mmHg at 6 hours, peaks at about 46 mmHg at 6.5 hours when the fascia is slit, then drops to about 12 mmHg by 7 hours and settles near 8 mmHg. A dashed line at 30 mmHg marks a common working danger level, and a line at 90 mmHg marks the average pressure in the main artery, which the compartment never approaches.

hlines.label: a common working danger level, 30 mmHg
average pressure in the main artery

questions.q: Read the compartment pressure 6 hours after the fracture.
questions.why: About 44 mmHg, several times the normal resting level of under 10 mmHg. The deep fascia cannot stretch, so the bleeding and swelling keep pushing it up.

questions.q: About how many hours after the fracture does the pressure reach the 30 mmHg danger level?
questions.why: About 4 hours. From there on, capillary flow in the compartment is at risk; muscle and nerve can start to die within hours unless the pressure is relieved.

questions.q: During which stretch are the muscles in the compartment most at risk of being starved of oxygen?
options: From 4 to 6.5 hours
From 0 to 4 hours, while the pressure first rises
After 6.5 hours, once the fascia is slit
At no time, because the artery stays open

why.correct: Once the compartment pressure is high enough, the veins are squeezed shut and capillary flow fails, so oxygen cannot reach the muscle even though blood still arrives in the artery.
options: Right: high compartment pressure stops capillary flow.
The pressure is rising here, but it is still low enough for capillary flow to continue.
Slitting the fascia lets the pressure fall and blood flow return.
The artery staying open is exactly the trap: blood reaches the compartment in the artery, but cannot pass through the squeezed capillaries.

questions.q: At 6 hours, a foot pulse can still be felt. What does the graph show that explains this?
options: The artery’s pressure stays far above it
The pressure has already fallen by 6 hours
The artery lies outside every compartment
The pulse is felt before the fracture reaches the artery

why.correct: The main artery’s average pressure, about 90 mmHg, stays far above the 44 mmHg in the compartment, so the artery stays open and pulses while the low-pressure veins and capillaries are shut. A present pulse does not rule out compartment syndrome.
options: Right: arterial pressure is far higher than compartment pressure.
At 6 hours the pressure is near its peak; it falls only after the fascia is slit.
The leg’s main vessels run through the compartments; they are exposed to the same pressure.
The pulse has nothing to do with where the break is; it depends on the pressure inside the artery.

questions.q: Suppose the warning signs were missed and no surgery was done. How would the curve after 6.5 hours differ?
options: It keeps climbing above the danger level
It falls back by itself as the fascia stretches
It levels off just below 30 mmHg
It drops to 0 mmHg

why.correct: Nothing has changed the fixed volume: the fascia still cannot stretch, the veins stay shut, and starved, swelling tissue adds more fluid. The pressure stays high or climbs, and muscle and nerve die.
options: Right: only opening the fascia relieves the pressure.
Deep fascia is dense collagen that barely stretches; that is why the pressure rose in the first place.
With the veins squeezed shut, trapped fluid keeps the pressure rising rather than settling below the danger level.
Tissue pressure cannot fall below its normal level of a few mmHg, and nothing here would lower it.

graphs.title: Hip, knee and ankle angles in one stride
graphs.intro: Joint angles at the hip, knee and ankle, measured from the side through one stride of normal walking, starting as the heel touches the ground. Zero is anatomical position. For the hip and knee, positive values are flexion; for the ankle, positive is dorsiflexion and negative is plantar flexion. The foot is on the ground for the first 60% of the stride and in the air for the rest. Values are typical for a healthy adult walking at a comfortable speed.
graphs.alt: Three stacked line graphs sharing an x axis of 0 to 100% of one stride; the foot is on the ground from 0 to 60% and in the air from 60 to 100%. Hip: 30 degrees of flexion at heel contact, falling steadily to about 10 degrees behind anatomical position at 55%, then rising to about 32 degrees of flexion at 85 to 90% and ending at 30. Knee: 4 degrees at heel contact, a small bend to about 19 degrees at 15%, nearly straight at about 3 degrees at 40%, then bending to a peak of about 62 degrees at 73% while the foot is in the air, and straightening to 4 degrees by the next heel contact. Ankle: 0 at heel contact, about 7 degrees of plantar flexion at 8%, then dorsiflexion to about 10 degrees at 46%, then plantar flexion to about 17 degrees at 63% as the toes push off, returning to about 0 through the air phase.

questions.q: Read the largest knee angle in the stride. How far is the knee flexed at that moment?
questions.why: About 62 degrees, reached while the foot is in the air. Bending the knee shortens the leg so the foot clears the ground as it swings forward.

questions.q: How far is the hip flexed at the moment the heel touches the ground?
questions.why: About 30 degrees of flexion: the thigh has been carried forward, in the sagittal plane, ahead of the body to reach for the next step.

questions.q: What is the greatest dorsiflexion at the ankle while the foot is on the ground?
questions.why: About 10 degrees, near 46% of the stride. With the foot flat, the body rolls forward over it, so the shin tips toward the top of the foot: dorsiflexion at the talocrural joint.

questions.q: From about 73% to 97% of the stride, the knee line falls toward zero. Which movement is the knee making, and why then?
options: Flexion, bending the knee to lift the foot clear of the ground
Extension, straightening for heel contact
Hyperextension, locking the knee back past straight
Medial rotation of the tibia on the femur, turning the foot in

why.correct: A falling knee angle means the angle between thigh and leg is getting larger: extension. The leg straightens as it swings forward so the heel can land with the knee nearly straight.
options: Flexion makes the angle smaller; here it is getting larger. The flexion that clears the foot comes earlier, up to about 73%.
Right: the angle is opening, which is extension, in time for heel contact.
The line stops at about 4 degrees of flexion and never goes below zero, so the knee does not pass straight.
This graph shows only sagittal-plane angles, and the knee rotates only a little, and only when bent. The change seen here is extension.

questions.q: In which stretch does the ankle plant flex sharply, pushing the toes against the ground just before they leave it?
options: From about 46% to 63% of the stride
From heel contact to about 8%, as the foot lowers
From about 20% to 46%, while the foot is flat
From about 80% to 100%

why.correct: The ankle line drops from about 10 degrees of dorsiflexion to about 17 degrees of plantar flexion as the heel lifts and the toes press down, then the toes leave the ground at 60%.
options: Right: the steep fall of the ankle line is plantar flexion at push-off.
There is a small plantar flexion as the foot lowers to the ground after heel contact, but it is only about 7 degrees and does not push off.
Here the line rises: the ankle dorsiflexes as the body rolls forward over the flat foot.
In the air the ankle returns to about neutral so the toes clear the ground.

questions.q: In which stretch is the hip line below zero, and what does that mean for the thigh?
options: At heel contact: the thigh is flexed farthest forward
While the foot is in the air: the thigh is swinging back
From about 45% to 63%: extended past anatomical position, behind the body
At 100%: the hip has returned to anatomical position

why.correct: Zero is anatomical position, so negative values mean extension carried past it: the thigh trails behind the body as the other leg steps forward. It peaks at about 10 degrees near 55%.
options: At heel contact the hip is at about 30 degrees of flexion, the most forward point, not below zero.
In the air phase the hip line rises: the thigh swings forward, which is flexion.
Right: extension past anatomical position, with the thigh behind the body.
