At 100% the hip is back at about 30 degrees of flexion, ready for the next heel contact.

questions.q: A patient walks with a brace that locks his knee straight. How does his knee line change?
options: It keeps its shape but shifts up by about 10 degrees
It becomes a flat line near zero
Its peak moves later, but reaches the same height
It is unchanged, because the brace acts only on the hip

why.correct: A locked knee cannot flex, so its angle stays near zero all stride. With no knee bend in the air, the leg stays long, and he must swing it out to the side or hitch the hip up so the foot clears the ground.
options: Shifting up would mean more flexion throughout; a locked brace allows none.
Right: no flexion at all, so the line is flat near zero.
Any peak means the knee is flexing, which a locked brace prevents.
The brace blocks the knee joint itself, the hinge between femur and tibia.

questions.q: A patient’s talocrural (ankle) joint has been fused in neutral. How does the ankle line change?
options: It flattens near zero all stride
Only the push-off dip disappears; the rise before it stays
It is unchanged, because the subtalar joint takes over tipping the foot up and down
It shifts down, so the ankle stays plantar flexed all stride

why.correct: Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion both happen at the talocrural joint, a hinge. Fused in neutral, it holds the angle near zero; the patient rolls over the foot with a stiffer, shorter push-off.
options: Right: the hinge that makes both movements is fused, so both are lost.
Both the rise and the dip are the same hinge moving, so fusion removes both.
The subtalar joint turns the sole inward and outward; it cannot tip the foot up and down.
Fused in neutral means held at zero, not plantar flexed.

graphs.title: Cartilage under load and after
graphs.intro: A schematic of how thick knee cartilage is, compared with its rested thickness, while a person carries a steady load for 30 minutes and then lies down for 90 minutes. The scale, a few percent thinner under load and a recovery lasting an hour or more, matches what imaging studies of loaded knee cartilage report; exact values vary with the joint, the load and the person.
graphs.alt: A line graph of change in cartilage thickness, in percent, against time from 0 to 120 minutes. Under load, from 0 to 30 minutes, thickness falls quickly at first and then more slowly: about minus 2.6% at 5 minutes, minus 3.5% at 10, minus 4.5% at 20 and minus 4.9% at 30. After the load is removed at 30 minutes, it recovers, quickly at first and then slowly: about minus 3.1% at 40 minutes, minus 1.4% at 60, minus 0.6% at 80 and back to 0 by 120.

questions.q: Read the change in cartilage thickness at the end of the 30 minutes of load.
questions.why: About 5% thinner (a change of about minus 5%). The thickness lost is fluid squeezed out of the cartilage by the load.

questions.q: Half an hour after the load comes off, at 60 minutes, what is the change in thickness?
questions.why: About minus 1.4%: most of the loss has been made up, but not all. Fluid returns more slowly as the cartilage nears its rested thickness.

questions.q: During which stretch is synovial fluid being drawn back into the cartilage?
options: While the load is on, from 0 to 30 minutes
After the load is removed, from 30 minutes on
Only in the first 5 minutes
At no point; cartilage is refilled from its blood vessels

why.correct: When the load comes off, the cartilage springs back toward its shape and draws fresh synovial fluid in, so thickness rises. That fresh fluid carries oxygen and nutrients to the chondrocytes.
options: Under load, thickness falls: fluid is being pushed out, not drawn in.
Right: the rising line after unloading is fluid returning.
The first 5 minutes are the fastest loss, when fluid is squeezed out most quickly.
Articular cartilage has no blood vessels; all its fluid exchange is with synovial fluid.

questions.q: When is fluid leaving the cartilage fastest?
options: In the first few minutes of loading
Just before the load is removed, at 25 to 30 minutes
Right after the load is removed, as the line turns up
At the end of the rest period

why.correct: The line is steepest at the start: loading first squeezes fluid out quickly, and the outflow slows as the cartilage gets denser and the remaining fluid is harder to push out.
options: Right: the steepest downward slope is at the start of the load.
By 25 to 30 minutes the line is nearly flat, so little fluid is still leaving.
After unloading, the line rises: fluid is coming back in, not leaving.
By the end of rest the line is flat at zero; no fluid is leaving.

questions.q: The same person carries a much heavier load for the same 30 minutes. How does the loaded part of the curve change?
options: It is unchanged, because cartilage does not compress
It falls less, because a heavier load seals the fluid in
It falls faster and deeper
It rises above zero, because load draws fluid in

why.correct: A heavier load presses harder on the cartilage, squeezing more fluid out and faster, so it thins more. Removing the load then lets it recover in the same way.
options: Cartilage is slightly compressible; that is what the loaded curve shows.
More pressure pushes more fluid out, not less.
Right: more load, more fluid pushed out, a deeper curve.
Load squeezes fluid out; fluid is drawn in only when the load comes off.

graphs.title: One stimulus: action potential, calcium and force
graphs.intro: One skeletal muscle fiber is stimulated once at time zero. From the top: the membrane potential of its sarcolemma, the calcium level in its sarcoplasm and the force it produces. Calcium and force are drawn as a percent of their own peaks. Values are typical, not from one fiber.
graphs.alt: Three stacked graphs over 150 ms. Top: the membrane potential rests at −90 mV, spikes to +30 mV at about 2 ms and is back at −90 mV by 5 ms. Middle: calcium rises from zero to its peak at about 8 ms, then falls, to about 30 percent by 30 ms and near zero by 60 ms. Bottom: force stays at zero for the first 5 ms, rises to its peak at about 35 ms and falls slowly, to about 10 percent by 100 ms and zero by about 135 ms.

questions.q: At about what time after the stimulus does force peak?
questions.why: About 35 ms, long after the action potential ended at about 5 ms and after calcium has already started to fall. Force lags because the filaments must first take up the slack in the tendon and connective tissue.

questions.q: At about what time does calcium in the sarcoplasm peak?
questions.why: About 8 ms, a few milliseconds after the action potential. The action potential runs down the T tubules, the voltage sensors pull the release channels open, and calcium floods out of the SR within milliseconds.

questions.q: Between about 10 and 60 ms, the calcium trace falls back toward rest. What is happening to the calcium?
options: The SR’s pumps split ATP to move it back into the SR
It diffuses out of the fiber into the extracellular fluid
Troponin absorbs it and breaks it down
The T tubules carry it back to the surface of the fiber

why.correct: The release channels closed when the action potential ended, and the calcium pumps in the SR membrane, each a calcium ATPase, return calcium to the SR against its gradient. That takes tens of milliseconds.
options: Right: active transport back into the SR.
The calcium came from the SR, and it goes back there; it is not lost from the fiber.
Troponin binds calcium and lets it go again; nothing breaks calcium down.
The T tubules carry the electrical signal, not calcium. Their inside is extracellular fluid.

questions.q: The action potential is over by about 5 ms, yet force keeps rising until about 35 ms. Over that stretch, what keeps the filaments pulling?
options: Calcium is still bound to troponin, and ATP keeps the heads cycling
The action potential keeps running along the T tubules for 30 ms
Tropomyosin actively pushes the thin filaments inward
The SR keeps releasing calcium until force peaks

why.correct: Calcium has not yet been pumped away, so troponin keeps tropomyosin off actin, and with ATP the heads bind, pull and recock again and again. Force builds while they take up the slack.
options: Right: calcium on troponin plus ATP keeps the cycle going.
Each action potential lasts only 2 to 5 ms, in the T tubules as on the surface.
Tropomyosin is a blocker, not a motor; the myosin heads do the pulling.
The release channels close as soon as the membrane returns to rest; calcium is already falling well before force peaks.

questions.q: The fiber is treated with dantrolene, which blocks the SR release channels, and stimulated again. How do the calcium and force curves change?
options: Both are much smaller; the action potential is unchanged
Calcium is unchanged, but force is smaller
Both last much longer, at the same height
The action potential disappears, so both stay flat

why.correct: The sarcolemma still fires, but the voltage sensors cannot pull the blocked channels open, so little calcium leaves the SR. Less calcium on troponin means fewer heads can bind, and force falls.
options: Right: less release, less force.
Force depends on calcium; if calcium were unchanged, force would be too.
That is what blocking the pumps would do. Dantrolene blocks release, so there is less calcium, not calcium that lingers.
Dantrolene acts on the SR, not on the voltage-gated channels of the sarcolemma, so the action potential still fires.

questions.q: Instead, a drug blocks the SR calcium pumps just before the stimulus. How do the calcium and force curves change?
options: Calcium stays high and force stays up long after 60 ms
Calcium peaks higher and falls faster
Calcium never rises, so there is no force
Nothing changes, because the pumps work only at rest

why.correct: Release is normal, but nothing returns the calcium to the SR. It stays on troponin, the heads keep cycling while ATP lasts, and the fiber cannot relax.
options: Right: without the pumps there is no relaxation.
The pumps do not affect how much calcium is released; they only remove it afterward.
Release goes through the release channels, which still open normally.
The pumps are what bring calcium down after every release; blocking them is what keeps it high.

graphs.title: One muscle twitch
graphs.intro: A myogram of one twitch: the tension of a motor unit of slow fibers after a single stimulus at time zero, drawn as a percent of its own peak. Values are typical.
graphs.alt: Tension against time over 150 ms. Tension stays at zero for about the first 5 ms, rises to its peak at about 35 ms, then falls more slowly, to about 40 percent by 75 ms, 13 percent by 100 ms and near zero by 150 ms.

questions.q: At about what time does tension peak?
questions.why: About 35 ms. Tension climbs while cross-bridges cycle and the elastic parts are pulled taut, and it peaks once calcium is being pumped back faster than it is released.

questions.q: The myogram stays flat for the first few milliseconds. Which phase is this, and what is happening?
options: The latent period: the action potential spreads and calcium is released
The relaxation phase: calcium is pumped back into the SR
The latent period: the fiber is refractory and cannot respond
The contraction phase: cross-bridges pull but the filaments do not slide

why.correct: In the latent period the action potential runs along the sarcolemma and down the T tubules, the SR releases calcium and cross-bridges begin taking up slack. The chemistry is under way, but tension has not shown yet.
options: Right: the hidden period.
Relaxation comes last, after the peak.
It is the latent period, but not because the fiber is refractory: the fiber has just fired, and the events that follow its action potential are what fill this time.
In the contraction phase tension rises; here it has not started.

questions.q: Which phase lasts longest, and why?
options: Relaxation, because pumping calcium back is slower than releasing it
Contraction, because cross-bridges cycle slowly in slow fibers
Relaxation, because the fiber must wait for its refractory period to end
The latent period, because acetylcholine takes time to cross the cleft

why.correct: Calcium floods out of the SR through open channels in milliseconds, but the pumps must return it against a steep gradient, which takes much longer. Tension fades as calcium leaves troponin.
options: Right: the pumps set the pace of relaxation.
Here the contraction phase is about 30 ms, shorter than the relaxation phase.
The refractory period is over within a few milliseconds; relaxation waits on the calcium pumps.
The latent period is the shortest phase, only a few milliseconds.

questions.q: How would the twitch of a fast fiber differ from this slow fiber’s twitch?
options: Shorter: it peaks sooner and is over far sooner
Longer: it rises more slowly but lasts longer
The same timing, but twice as tall
The same shape, but it starts later

why.correct: Fast fibers make myosin that splits ATP faster, so their cross-bridges cycle faster, and they pump calcium back into the SR faster. A fast fiber’s twitch can be over in about a third of the time.
options: Right: faster myosin and faster pumps.
That describes a slower fiber, not a fast one.
The y axis is a percent of each twitch’s own peak; what differs between fiber types here is timing.
A fast fiber starts sooner, not later.

graphs.title: Twitch, summation and tetanus
graphs.intro: The tension of one muscle fiber over one second, as a percent of its maximum. The lower strip marks each stimulus: first a single stimulus, then two stimuli 40 ms apart, then 20 stimuli per second, then 100 per second. Values are from a simple model with typical proportions.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over 1000 ms. The lower strip shows stimuli: one at 0 ms, two at 200 and 240 ms, then evenly spaced stimuli every 50 ms from 400 to 650 ms and every 10 ms from 750 to 1000 ms. Above, tension from one stimulus rises to a peak of about 25 percent and falls back. Two close stimuli give a higher peak of about 36 percent. At 20 per second, tension climbs in waves to a wavy plateau between about 27 and 35 percent. At 100 per second, tension climbs smoothly to a flat plateau of about 100 percent.

questions.q: Read the peak tension of the single twitch.
questions.why: About 25 percent of maximum. The pumps clear the calcium before the cross-bridges have pulled the fiber’s elastic parts fully taut, so a single twitch reaches only a fraction of what the fiber can do.

questions.q: Complete tetanus reaches about 100 percent. About how many times the single twitch’s peak is that?
questions.why: 100 ÷ 25 = 4. Complete tetanus is often three to five times the tension of one twitch, although each action potential releases about the same pulse of calcium.

questions.q: In which stretch does the fiber relax a little between stimuli, giving a wavy plateau?
options: At 20 stimuli per second
At 100 stimuli per second
After the single stimulus
After the two close stimuli

why.correct: That is incomplete (unfused) tetanus: stimuli come often enough for tension to build, but calcium falls a little between them, so each wave dips slightly.
options: Right: incomplete tetanus.
At 100 per second the fiber has no time to relax at all: complete tetanus, a smooth plateau.
After a single stimulus the fiber relaxes fully; there is no plateau.
Two close stimuli make one summed peak, not a plateau.

questions.q: Why does the second of two close stimuli produce a higher peak than a single twitch?
options: Calcium is released again before the first pulse has been pumped back
The second action potential releases twice as much calcium
More motor units are recruited by the second stimulus
The second action potential is larger than the first

why.correct: That is wave summation. Calcium stays high for longer, cross-bridges keep cycling, the elastic parts are pulled more taut, and tension climbs higher than one twitch can reach.
options: Right: calcium stays high for longer.
Each action potential releases about the same calcium; it is the timing that changes.
This is one fiber; recruitment adds motor units to a whole muscle.
Action potentials are all-or-none: every one is the same size.

questions.q: The rate in the stretch from 400 to 650 ms is raised from 20 to 40 stimuli per second. How does that part of the curve change?
options: Higher, with smaller ripples
Lower, because the fiber tires faster
Higher, with bigger ripples
Unchanged, because each twitch is all-or-none

why.correct: Stimuli now come every 25 ms instead of 50, so less calcium is cleared between them. Tension builds higher and the dips shrink, moving toward complete tetanus.
options: Right: toward fusion.
Over a quarter of a second, a fiber does not fatigue noticeably; the faster rate builds more tension.
Ripples shrink, not grow, because there is less time to relax between stimuli.
Each action potential is all-or-none, but more of them per second keeps calcium higher, and tension sums.

graphs.title: The length–tension relationship
graphs.intro: The active tension a muscle fiber can produce when stimulated into complete tetanus at different sarcomere lengths, as a percent of its maximum. Sarcomere length is a percent of resting length.
graphs.alt: Active tension against sarcomere length from 60 to 180 percent of resting length. Tension is zero at 60 percent, climbs steeply to about 80 percent of maximum at 80 percent length and to the maximum by 95 percent, stays flat at the maximum to 110 percent, then falls in a straight line to 50 percent at 140 percent length and zero at 170 percent.

questions.q: Read the tension the fiber can produce at 140 percent of resting length.
questions.why: About 50 percent. The thin filaments have been pulled partway off the thick filaments, so only about half as many myosin heads can reach actin.

questions.q: At what sarcomere length does active tension reach zero on the stretched side?
questions.why: About 170 percent. At that length the thin filaments no longer overlap the thick filaments at all, so no myosin head can bind actin and the fiber can produce no active tension.

questions.q: Where does the fiber produce its greatest tension, and why?
options: Around resting length, where the most myosin heads can reach actin
At the longest lengths, where the filaments are stretched tightest
At the shortest lengths, where the filaments overlap most
Anywhere, because tension does not depend on length

why.correct: Near resting length, the thin filaments overlap the whole part of each thick filament that carries heads, without yet meeting in the middle, so the largest number of cross-bridges can form.
options: Right: optimal overlap.
Stretching pulls the thin filaments off the thick ones, so fewer heads reach actin and tension falls.
At short lengths the thin filaments crowd past each other and the thick filaments butt against the Z discs, so tension falls steeply.
The curve shows a strong dependence on length, set by filament overlap.

questions.q: On the short side, tension falls steeply below about 80 percent. What causes that fall?
options: Thin filaments crowd past each other and thick filaments butt against the Z discs
The thin filaments slide off the ends of the thick filaments
The sarcomere runs out of ATP when it is short
Calcium cannot reach troponin in a short sarcomere

why.correct: When the sarcomere is too short, the thin filaments from the two ends overlap each other in the middle and get in each other’s way, and the thick filaments hit the Z discs. Tension reaches zero at about 60 percent.
options: Right: crowding and collision.
Sliding off the thick filaments happens on the stretched side, at long lengths.
ATP supply does not depend on sarcomere length.
Calcium release and binding are the same at every length on this curve; overlap is what changes.

questions.q: The whole muscle is tested the same way, but only half of its motor units are stimulated. Plotted as a percent of what the whole muscle can produce, how does the curve change?
options: Half as tall, with its peak at the same length
Same height, with its peak moved to longer lengths
Half as tall, with its peak moved to shorter lengths
Unchanged, because every fiber is at the same length

why.correct: Each stimulated fiber still follows the same overlap rule, so the shape and the optimal length stay the same. With half the fibers pulling, the tension at every length is halved.
options: Right: fewer fibers, same overlap rule.
Where the peak sits is set by filament overlap in each sarcomere, which recruitment does not change.
The optimal length does not move; only the height changes.
Every fiber is at the same length, but fewer of them are pulling, so the total tension is lower.

graphs.title: Energy systems over the first minutes of exercise
graphs.intro: During three minutes of all-out exercise. Top: the share of the ATP spent in the working muscle that each energy system supplies. Bottom: the ATP and creatine phosphate left in the working fibers, as a percent of their resting levels. Values are typical and vary with the person and the task.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over 180 seconds. Top: stored ATP and creatine phosphate supply about 85 percent of the ATP at the start, falling to about 22 percent by 20 seconds and near zero after a minute. Anaerobic glycolysis starts at about 12 percent, peaks at about 56 percent around 20 seconds and then declines to about 14 percent by 3 minutes. Aerobic respiration starts at about 3 percent, rises steadily, crosses glycolysis at about 75 seconds and reaches about 85 percent by 3 minutes. Bottom: creatine phosphate falls to about 50 percent of resting by 10 seconds and about 15 percent by a minute. ATP falls only slowly, to about 75 percent of resting by 90 seconds, and stays there.

x.label: Time from the start of all-out exercise

questions.q: At about what time does aerobic respiration overtake anaerobic glycolysis?
questions.why: At about 75 seconds, a minute and a quarter in. Aerobic respiration runs from the first second but is slow to reach full speed, because oxygen delivery and its many steps take time.

questions.q: Read how far ATP in the fibers has fallen by the end, as a percent of its resting level.
questions.why: Only to about 75 percent, about three quarters. The fiber remakes ATP almost as fast as it spends it, and fatigue slows the cross-bridges and calcium release before ATP can fall far. If ATP ran out, the heads could not let go of actin.

questions.q: During which stretch does anaerobic glycolysis supply the largest share of the ATP?
options: From about 10 to 75 seconds
The first 10 seconds
After about 75 seconds
It supplies the same share throughout

why.correct: Glycolysis speeds up within seconds, peaks around 20 seconds and leads until aerobic respiration overtakes it. A 400 m run falls in this stretch.
options: Right: roughly 10 seconds to a minute and a quarter.
In the first seconds creatine phosphate supplies most of the new ATP, fastest of all.
After 75 seconds aerobic respiration leads, and glycolysis keeps declining.
Every system’s share changes; only their total stays at 100 percent.

questions.q: What does the top panel show about the first 10 seconds?
options: All three systems are already running, with creatine phosphate leading
Only creatine phosphate is running; the others switch on later
Glycolysis supplies most of the ATP from the first second
Aerobic respiration supplies nothing until creatine phosphate is gone

why.correct: The systems overlap rather than taking turns. Creatine phosphate dominates at first because one fast reaction remakes ATP right beside the heads, but glycolysis and aerobic respiration are running and climbing from the first second.
options: Right: all three from the start.
All three lines are above zero from the start; the relay picture is wrong.
Glycolysis rises fast but does not lead until about 10 seconds.
Aerobic respiration is small at first but present from the first second.

questions.q: The same person walks briskly for three minutes instead. How does the aerobic respiration curve change?
options: It rises much sooner and supplies nearly all the ATP after a minute or two
It stays the same, because the systems always switch at 75 seconds
It falls, because gentle exercise uses creatine phosphate
It never rises, because walking needs no ATP

why.correct: At a gentle pace, ATP demand is low enough for the mitochondria to meet it almost alone once oxygen delivery rises: over 95 percent of the ATP comes from aerobic respiration after the first minutes.
options: Right: gentle work is aerobic.
The crossover time depends on how hard the work is; at a gentle pace there is little glycolysis to overtake.
Creatine phosphate covers only the first seconds of any effort, and gentle work spends it slowly.
All muscle work needs ATP; the question is which system supplies it.

graphs.title: The stretch response of smooth muscle
graphs.intro: A strip of bladder wall (smooth muscle) and a relaxed skeletal muscle are each suddenly stretched to 130 percent of their starting length at 10 seconds and held there. The graph shows their tension, as a percent of the peak just after the stretch. Values are typical.
graphs.alt: Tension against time over 120 seconds. Both start at 20 percent. At 10 seconds both jump to 100 percent. The skeletal muscle line drops only slightly, to about 92 percent, and stays there. The smooth muscle line falls back steadily, to about 50 percent by 28 seconds and about 23 percent by 70 seconds, close to where it started, although it is still stretched.

questions.q: Read the smooth muscle’s tension at 70 seconds.
questions.why: About 22 percent, back near its starting 20 percent, although the strip is still held 30 percent longer. That fall is stress-relaxation.

questions.q: In the stretch held from 10 to 70 seconds, what is the smooth muscle doing?
options: Stress-relaxation: its filaments rearrange and tension falls back at the new length
Tetanus: its tension sums to a plateau
Losing its stretch: the strip shortens back to its starting length
Fatigue: it runs out of ATP and gives up

why.correct: After a stretch, smooth muscle slowly lets its tension fall back while it stays at the new length, as its filaments and cross-bridges rearrange and the fibers settle at the longer length.
options: Right: the stress-relaxation response.
Tetanus is a rise in tension from rapid stimulation; here tension falls.
The strip is held at 130 percent the whole time; only its tension changes.
Tension falls without any loss of ATP; the strip can still contract strongly at the new length.

questions.q: How does the smooth muscle curve explain why pressure in a filling bladder stays low?
options: After each stretch the wall’s tension falls back, so the wall fits each new volume without squeezing harder
The bladder wall is skeletal muscle, which keeps its tension low
The stretch makes the wall contract, pushing urine out as it arrives
Smooth muscle cannot produce tension once it has been stretched

why.correct: As urine slowly stretches the wall, stress-relaxation lets its tension return toward the starting level at each new length, so the pressure inside barely rises from 50 to 400 mL.
options: Right: stress-relaxation lets the bladder store.
The bladder wall is smooth muscle; the skeletal muscle line keeps its tension high.
A sudden stretch can trigger a contraction, but a slow, sustained stretch is met by stress-relaxation, and storage organs mostly relax as they fill.
Smooth muscle produces force over a wide range of lengths, so a full bladder still contracts strongly.

questions.q: At 70 seconds the smooth muscle strip is stretched a second time, by the same amount, and held. How does its curve continue?
options: Tension jumps again, then falls back most of the way once more
Tension jumps and stays high this time
Tension does not change, because the strip has already relaxed
Tension falls below its starting level

why.correct: Each new stretch raises tension at once, and each is met by stress-relaxation. That is how a filling bladder relaxes to fit every new volume.
options: Right: the same response at the new length.
Staying high is how skeletal muscle responds; smooth muscle relaxes again.
The new stretch raises tension at first, before it falls back.
Tension falls back toward, not below, its level before the stretch.

graphs.title: Heat loss at rest as the air warms
graphs.intro: A resting person makes about 100 W of heat, and to hold body temperature steady must lose exactly that much. The graph shows how the loss is shared between the dry routes (radiation, conduction and convection together) and evaporation as the air warms. It is a simplified model of a lightly clothed person in still, dry air; the numbers are rounded to show the pattern. Below zero, a route adds heat instead of removing it.
graphs.alt: Two lines plotted against air temperature from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius, on a heat axis from minus 60 to 160 watts. The dry-routes line stays near 80 watts from 20 to 26 degrees, falls steeply from about 74 watts at 28 degrees to zero at 35 degrees, and keeps falling below zero to minus 50 watts at 40 degrees. The evaporation line is the mirror image: about 20 watts from 20 to 26 degrees, rising steeply to 100 watts at 35 degrees and 150 watts at 40 degrees. A horizontal line marks the 100 watts of heat made at rest.

hlines.label: heat made at rest, about 100 W

questions.q: In air at 20 °C, how much heat does evaporation remove?
questions.why: About 20 W, a fifth of the total. In a cool room most heat leaves by radiation, conduction and convection, and evaporation is mainly water lost from the airways and through the skin without visible sweat.

questions.q: At what air temperature do the dry routes stop removing heat?
questions.why: About 35 °C, the temperature of the skin. Heat always moves down a temperature gradient, so once the air is as warm as the skin there is no gradient for radiation, conduction or convection to use.

questions.q: In air at 38 °C, how much heat must evaporation remove to keep body temperature steady?
questions.why: About 130 W: the 100 W the body makes plus the 30 W the hot air now adds by radiation and convection. Evaporation has to remove more heat than the body makes.

questions.q: In which range is evaporation the only way left to lose heat?
options: Above about 35 °C, where the air is hotter than the skin
Between 20 and 28 °C, where evaporation is lowest
Between 28 and 35 °C, where sweating rises steeply
At every temperature, since sweat is always the main route

why.correct: Once the air is hotter than the skin, radiation, conduction and convection run backward and add heat. Evaporation is the only route that can only remove heat, so it must carry the whole load and more.
options: Right: above skin temperature only evaporation removes heat.
In cool air the dry routes remove most of the heat; evaporation is small.
Here sweating rises, but the dry routes still remove some heat until the air reaches skin temperature.
In a cool room evaporation removes only about a fifth of the heat; the dry routes do most of the work.

questions.q: In which range does the body hold heat loss steady mainly by adjusting dermal blood flow, with little sweating?
options: From about 20 to 28 °C
From about 28 to 35 °C
From about 35 to 40 °C

why.correct: Across this range the dry routes stay near 80 W even though the air warms. Narrowing or widening the dermal vessels sets how warm the skin is, and so the size of the gradient to the air, without needing sweat.
options: Right: dermal blood flow does the work in cool to mild air.
Here the dry routes fall steeply and sweating has to make up the difference.
Here the dry routes add heat, so sweating has to remove it all.

questions.q: In humid air, the sweat on the skin can evaporate only slowly. How does the evaporation line change?
options: It levels off at a lower height, so above about 33 °C heat builds up
It rises more steeply, because humid air makes you sweat more
It does not change, because the sweat glands still secrete
It moves to the left, so sweating starts at a lower temperature

why.correct: Evaporation needs air that can take up more water vapor. Humid air cannot, so however hard the glands work, evaporation stops rising. Once the heat to be removed passes what evaporation can manage, the body stores heat and its temperature climbs.
options: Right: evaporation hits a ceiling.
The glands may secrete more, but sweat that cannot evaporate drips off and removes almost no heat.
Secreting sweat is not the same as removing heat; only evaporating sweat cools.
Humidity does not change when sweating starts; it limits how much of the sweat evaporates.

graphs.title: Strength of a healing wound
graphs.intro: The strength of a healing skin wound, as a percentage of the strength of unwounded skin, over the six months after the injury. The values are approximate: they come from classic measurements, and studies differ, especially in the first week.
graphs.alt: Wound strength as a percentage of unwounded skin plotted against weeks after injury, from 0 to 24 weeks. Strength is near zero at first, about 8 percent at week 1 and 22 percent at week 3, rises steeply to about 60 percent by week 8 and 72 percent by week 12, then levels off near 79 percent at week 24. Horizontal lines mark unwounded skin at 100 percent and a ceiling of about 80 percent.

hlines.label: about the most a scar reaches

questions.q: Read the wound’s strength 3 weeks after the injury.
questions.why: About a fifth of normal. The wound is closed and covered by new epidermis, but its collagen is still young and loosely arranged, which is why a healing wound must be protected from strain for weeks.

questions.q: Read the wound’s strength 12 weeks after the injury.
questions.why: About 70%. Collagen laid down in the first weeks is being reorganized and cross-linked, so strength keeps rising even though little new tissue is added.

questions.q: During which stretch is the wound weakest, held together mainly by the clot, or by stitches if it was closed?
options: The first week
Weeks 1 to 8
Weeks 8 to 24

why.correct: In the first days, bleeding stops and inflammation clears the wound. Almost no collagen has been laid down yet, so the clot, and any stitches, hold the edges.
options: Right: little collagen yet.
In these weeks fibroblasts lay down collagen, and strength climbs fastest.
By now the wound has much of its final strength and is being remodeled.

questions.q: Strength keeps creeping up for months after the wound has closed. In which stretch, and why?
options: Weeks 8 to 24: the collagen is reorganized and cross-linked
Weeks 8 to 24: new hair follicles and glands grow into the scar
Weeks 1 to 8: the scab hardens
The first week: the clot contracts

why.correct: In remodeling the collagen fibers are rearranged along the lines of stress and cross-linked, which strengthens the scar without adding much tissue. Most new capillaries disappear, and the scar pales.
options: Right: remodeling strengthens the collagen already there.
A scar never regrows hair follicles, sweat glands or sebaceous glands.
The scab falls off once new epidermis has formed; it adds no strength to the dermis.
The clot holds the wound only in the first days; the months-long rise comes from collagen.

questions.q: If you followed the wound for another year, where would the curve end up?
options: It levels off near 80%, never reaching unwounded skin
It keeps rising until it reaches 100%
It rises above 100%, because scar tissue is tougher
It falls back toward zero as the collagen is removed

why.correct: Even after a year or more of remodeling, a scar reaches at most about 80% of the strength of unwounded skin: its collagen is never arranged quite like the original dermis.
options: Right: a scar tops out at about 80%.
The collagen of a scar never matches the original arrangement, so it stays weaker.
Scar tissue is weaker than unwounded skin, not stronger.
Remodeling reorganizes collagen; it does not remove the scar.

questions.q: An infection prolongs the inflammation stage by about a week. How does the curve shift?
options: To the right: strength starts rising about a week later
Upward: the extra inflammation makes the scar stronger
To the left: the wound heals faster
It does not change, because infection affects only the surface

why.correct: Rebuilding cannot start in earnest until the wound is cleared of microbes and debris. Longer inflammation delays the laying down of collagen, so the whole rise comes later.
options: Right: the rise is delayed.
Inflammation clears the wound; it does not add strength, and prolonged inflammation can leave a worse scar.
Infection slows healing; it never speeds it up.
An infected wound is inflamed through its depth, which holds up every later stage.

graphs.title: Hair length through the growth cycle
graphs.intro: The length of one scalp hair and one eyelash, followed for four years from the start of a growth phase. In this example the scalp follicle stays in anagen for 3 years (it can be 2 to 7) and grows about 1 cm a month; the eyelash grows about 0.4 cm a month for 2.5 months, then rests about 4 months. Each drop is an old hair pushed out by a new one. Values are typical, not from one person.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over 48 months. Top, scalp hair: length rises steadily from 0 to 36 centimeters over 36 months, stays at 36 centimeters from month 36 to about month 39.5, then the old hair is shed and a new hair grows from 0 to about 9 centimeters by month 48. Bottom, eyelash: a sawtooth in which the lash grows from 0 to 1 centimeter over 2.5 months, stays at 1 centimeter for 4 months, then drops to 0 as it is shed, repeating about every 6.5 months.

questions.q: How long is the scalp hair after 12 months?
questions.why: About 12 cm. During anagen the matrix makes hair at about 1 cm a month, 0.3 to 0.4 mm a day, so a year of growth gives about 12 cm.

questions.q: What is the longest the eyelash gets?
questions.why: About 1 cm. The lash grows only two to three times more slowly than a scalp hair; it stays short mainly because its anagen phase ends after a couple of months.

questions.q: During which stretch are the matrix cells of the scalp follicle dividing?
options: Months 0 to 36
Months 36 to 39.5
Only in the last month before the hair is shed

why.correct: The hair lengthens only while its matrix divides, in anagen. The steady climb of the line is that growth.
options: Right: anagen is the growth phase.
Here the line is flat: the matrix has stopped (catagen) and the follicle is resting with its club hair (telogen).
Just before shedding the follicle is resting; the new hair that pushes the old one out grows in the next anagen.

questions.q: In which stretch does the scalp follicle hold a club hair that is no longer growing?
options: Months 36 to 39.5
Months 0 to 36
Months 39.5 to 48

why.correct: After anagen, the short catagen phase forms a hard club at the base of the hair, and the follicle then rests in telogen for about 3 months. The hair keeps its length but does not grow.
options: Right: catagen and telogen.
Here the matrix is dividing and the hair is growing.
Here a new hair is growing; the old club hair has been pushed out.

questions.q: At month 12, she starts a cancer drug that kills rapidly dividing cells. How does the scalp hair line change?
options: It stops rising and drops to zero within weeks
It keeps rising at the same rate
It levels off and the hair is held for 3 months, as in telogen
It rises faster as the follicle repairs itself

why.correct: The drug stops the matrix cells of anagen follicles. The weakened hair breaks or falls out within a few weeks, instead of passing through catagen and telogen. The follicle survives, so hair regrows after treatment.
options: Right: growth stops and the hair is lost within weeks.
Matrix cells are among the fastest-dividing cells in the body, so they are among the first hit.
The hair is lost quickly, without the resting phase of a normal cycle.
The drug stops division; nothing makes the hair grow faster.

questions.q: In another person, scalp anagen lasts 2 years instead of 3, with the same growth rate. How does the scalp line change?
options: It levels off at about 24 cm, a year earlier
It rises more slowly and reaches 36 cm later
It reaches 36 cm sooner by growing faster
It is the same, because hair length depends only on growth rate

why.correct: Maximum length = growth rate × time in anagen. At 1 cm a month for 24 months the hair reaches about 24 cm and then stops. That is why some people cannot grow their hair very long.
options: Right: a shorter anagen means a shorter maximum length.
The growth rate is the same; only the time spent growing changes.
Nothing changes the growth rate here; the hair stops a year sooner.
Length depends on both the rate and how long anagen lasts; the eyelash shows the same thing.

graphs.title: Bone mass across the lifespan
graphs.intro: Bone mass here is the mass of calcium in the whole skeleton, which tracks the amount of bone. The curves show typical values for men and women from birth to 100, following OpenStax Figure 6.23. Whether bone is gained, kept or lost depends on the balance between osteoblasts and osteoclasts at each age.
graphs.alt: Two curves of skeletal calcium in grams against age from 0 to 100 years. Both rise steeply through childhood and the teens. The male curve peaks at about 1,510 grams between 35 and 40 and falls slowly to about 1,020 grams at 100. The female curve peaks at about 1,220 grams at 35, falls slowly to about 1,100 grams at 50, then drops steeply to about 800 grams at 60, and falls slowly to about 545 grams at 100.

questions.q: Read the peak calcium content of the male skeleton.
questions.why: About 1,500 g, reached in the thirties. That is roughly the "kilogram or so" of calcium stored in an adult skeleton, the bank the blood draws on.

questions.q: At their peaks, how many more grams of calcium does the typical male skeleton hold than the female skeleton?
questions.why: About 1,510 − 1,220 = about 290 g. Men usually reach a higher peak, so women start their later losses from a lower level, one reason osteoporosis is more common in women.

questions.q: Read the calcium content of the female skeleton at 100.
questions.why: About 545 g, less than half her peak. Decades of remodeling cycles that each remove slightly more than they replace, plus the fast loss in her fifties, add up.

questions.q: During which ages does bone mass climb steeply, and why?
options: 30 to 40, when bone is added fastest because growth in length has stopped
40 to 60, when remodeling adds bone in preparation for old age
Birth to about 30, while formation outpaces resorption
At the same rate at every age, from birth to 100

why.correct: In childhood and the teens, osteoblasts build more than osteoclasts remove, and the growing skeleton adds bone quickly. Peak bone mass is reached by about 30.
options: The curves are flat from 30 to 40: formation and resorption are about equal at the peak.
From 40 on, each remodeling cycle removes slightly more than it replaces, so the curves fall.
Right: formation outpaces resorption through growth.
The curves rise, flatten and then fall, because the balance between osteoblasts and osteoclasts shifts with age.

questions.q: Where does the women’s curve suddenly fall faster, and what causes it?
options: Around 20 to 30, as the bones stop growing in length at the plates
Around 50 to 60, at the end of the reproductive years
Around 30 to 40, as the peak is passed and remodeling starts to lose bone
Around 80 to 100, as remodeling finally stops

why.correct: At the end of the reproductive years, the ovaries’ hormone that slows the formation and activity of osteoclasts falls. Resorption rises, and bone is lost fast for five to ten years.
options: Between 20 and 30 both curves are still rising toward their peaks.
Right: the end of the reproductive years.
Past the peak, loss is slow in both sexes; the sudden drop comes later, only in women.
Remodeling never stops, and late in life the curves fall slowly, not steeply.

questions.q: A girl eats little calcium and does little weight-bearing exercise through her teens. How does her curve change?
options: It rises less and peaks lower, and every later age starts from less bone
It rises the same way, because peak bone mass is set by her genes alone
It peaks at the same height, but later, at about 45 instead of 35
It peaks lower, but she then loses bone more slowly and catches up

why.correct: Bone is built in youth from the calcium you eat and from load. Less of each means a lower peak, and a lower peak leaves less bone to lose before it becomes fragile, which is why youth habits matter decades later.
options: Right: a lower peak, and a lower curve from then on.
Genes matter, but calcium and load through Wolff’s law also set how much bone is built.
The timing of the peak is about the same; it is the height of the peak that falls.
Losses after the peak follow the same balance of osteoblasts and osteoclasts, so she does not catch up.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man spends six months in bed. How does his curve change?
options: It stays on the usual line, because adult bone no longer changes
It rises, because bone at rest has time to rebuild without strain
It drops for those months, then partly recovers once he walks
It drops for good to the level of a typical 80-year-old

why.correct: Without load, osteocytes signal for less building and more resorption, and bone is lost quickly. When he walks again, load rebuilds some of it, but recovery is slower than the loss and often incomplete.
options: Adult bone is remodeled all the time, and load steers the balance, so unloading shows up within weeks.
Unloaded bone is resorbed faster, not rebuilt: Wolff’s law in reverse.
Right: a fast drop, then partial recovery.
The loss is a few percent, not decades’ worth, and some returns with walking.

graphs.title: Growth rate in height through childhood
graphs.intro: Height grows mostly by the lengthening of long bones at their epiphyseal plates. The curves show the typical growth rate, in centimeters of height gained per year, for girls and boys from 2 to 20. Values are typical averages; individual children vary by a year or two.
graphs.alt: Growth rate in centimeters per year against age from 2 to 20. Both curves start at about 10 at age 2 and fall to about 5.5 by age 8. The girls’ curve rises to a peak of about 8 at age 12, then falls to near 0 by about 17. The boys’ curve keeps falling to about 5 at 10 and 11, rises to a peak of about 9.5 at 14, and falls to near 0 by about 19.

questions.q: Read the boys’ highest growth rate during the growth spurt.
questions.why: About 9.5 cm a year, at about 14. The hormones of puberty speed chondrocyte division at the plates, nearly doubling the childhood rate for a year or two.

questions.q: At about what age do girls grow fastest?
questions.why: At about 12, roughly two years before boys. Girls start puberty earlier, so their spurt, and the closing of their plates, come earlier too.

questions.q: In the late teens both curves fall to zero. What is happening in the long bones?
options: The plates are closing: bone replaces their cartilage, leaving epiphyseal lines
The plates are still growing, but appositional growth has stopped
Osteoclasts are removing bone from the ends as fast as the plates add it
The diaphysis has run out of room to grow into the epiphysis

why.correct: Chondrocytes in the plates slow and stop dividing, bone replaces the last of the cartilage, and the epiphysis fuses with the diaphysis. With no plate left, the bone cannot grow longer. This happens mostly between 15 and 21, earlier in girls.
options: Right: the plates close.
Appositional growth makes bones wider and continues slowly for life; height stops because the plates close.
Osteoclasts clear old cartilage and bone below the plate, but length stops because the plate itself is gone.
The plate moves away from the middle of the bone like a treadmill; growth stops only when its cartilage is used up and replaced.

questions.q: Between 10 and 13, girls are growing faster than boys. Which statement explains the region highlighted?
options: Boys’ epiphyseal plates have already closed by this age
Boys are still in childhood growth; their spurt comes later
Boys’ bones grow only by appositional growth at this age
Girls’ chondrocytes enlarge at this age, but boys’ only divide

why.correct: Puberty, and with it the spurt, starts about two years earlier in girls. Boys keep growing at the slower childhood rate until their own spurt, which is taller and later, and they keep growing for longer.
options: Boys’ plates close later than girls’, not earlier; their curve reaches zero around 19.
Right: the boys’ spurt is later.
Boys are still lengthening at their plates; appositional growth only adds width.
In the spurt, chondrocytes both divide faster and enlarge, in girls and boys alike.

questions.q: A girl starts puberty at 7 instead of about 10. How does her curve change?
options: The spurt comes earlier, but growth goes on to the usual age
The spurt is taller, but it still comes at the usual age
It is unchanged, because the plates close at a fixed age
Spurt and end of growth both move about four years earlier

why.correct: The hormones of puberty first speed the plates, then close them. Starting early moves both events earlier, so she is tall at 9 but loses years of childhood growth and ends up shorter than expected.
options: The same hormones that cause the spurt later close the plates, so an early spurt means early closure.
Timing is what changes: the spurt starts with puberty.
Plates close when puberty’s hormones act on them, not at a fixed age.
Right: both the spurt and the end of growth move earlier.

graphs.title: Calcium and the calcium-raising hormone
graphs.intro: The cells of the four tiny glands behind the thyroid release more calcium-raising hormone when blood calcium is low and less when it is high. The curve shows the typical shape of that response in people: hormone release as a percentage of its maximum at each level of total blood calcium. Exact values vary between people.
graphs.alt: Hormone release in percent of maximum against total blood calcium from 7 to 12 mg/dL. Release is near 100% at 7 to 8 mg/dL, falls slowly to about 80% at 9, drops steeply through about 50% at 9.5 to about 25% at 10, and levels off near 10 to 12% above 10.5. The normal range, 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL, is marked.

questions.q: Read the hormone release at a total blood calcium of 8.5 mg/dL.
questions.why: About 92% of maximum. At the low edge of the normal range, the gland cells are already releasing nearly all the hormone they can, pulling calcium from bone and holding it in the kidneys.

questions.q: At what total blood calcium is hormone release half of its maximum?
questions.why: About 9.5 mg/dL, the middle of the normal range. The midpoint of the steep part sits at the set point, which is where the loop holds calcium.

questions.q: Why does it matter that the steepest part of the curve lies in the middle of the normal range?
options: The hormone has no effect while calcium stays within the normal range
Small changes near the set point cause large swings in release
Release changes most where calcium is dangerously low
It shows that high calcium makes the gland cells release more hormone

why.correct: Where the curve is steep, a change of a few tenths of a mg/dL swings hormone release by tens of percent. That strong response to small errors is why blood calcium is held within a few percent of its set point.
options: Within the range the hormone is working all the time; its level rises and falls with every small change.
Right: small errors, big responses.
At dangerously low calcium the curve is flat, because release is already near its maximum.
The curve slopes down: higher calcium means less hormone, the negative feedback.

questions.q: Cancer in a woman’s bones drives her calcium to 12 mg/dL. Which part of the curve is she on?
options: The flat right-hand part: her gland cells have cut release to near its floor
The steep middle: her hormone release is still falling fast
The flat left-hand part: her gland cells are releasing as much hormone as they can
Off the curve: high calcium stops the gland cells from sensing calcium

why.correct: Above about 10.5 mg/dL, release has fallen to a small floor that it cannot go below. The loop has done all it can; the calcium keeps rising because the tumor drives osteoclasts directly.
options: Right: release near its floor.
The steep part is inside the normal range; by 12 mg/dL release has almost bottomed out.
Maximum release happens when calcium is low, not high.
The gland cells still sense calcium perfectly; that is why they have cut their hormone release.

questions.q: A medicine makes the gland cells’ receptor protein bind calcium more easily. How does the curve shift?
options: Right: release falls only once calcium reaches higher levels
Up: release rises at every calcium level, raising calcium
